lessons.title: 1.1 Historical Background of Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Early Ideas about Matter

The word science comes from the Latin word "Scientia", which means knowledge. Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter. Long ago, Greek thinkers tried to explain what matter is made of.

  • Democritus (460–357 BC, Greek) presented the idea that matter is made of a smallest, indivisible particle — the atom.
  • Aristotle (428–347 BC, Greek) presented the theory of the form and structure of matter and gave the idea of four elements: fire, water, earth and air.
  • Plato (428–347 BC, Greek) suggested the term "element" for the basic constituents of matter.

Muslim Scientists

  • Jabir bin Hayyan (721–803 AD) invented experimental methods for preparing nitric acid and hydrochloric acid, and described methods of dyeing cloth.
  • Al-Razi (862–930 AD) prepared ethyl alcohol (wine) by the fermentation method.
  • Al-Beruni (973–1048 AD) determined the densities of different substances.
  • Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD) presented the sciences of medicine, philosophy and astronomy.

Modern Scientists

  • Robert Boyle (1627–1691) presented the idea that chemistry is a natural science and discovered the gas laws.
  • J. Priestley (1733–1804) discovered oxygen, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen chloride.
  • Scheele (1742–1786) discovered chlorine gas.
  • Cavendish (1731–1810) discovered hydrogen gas.
  • Lavoisier (1743–1794) discovered that air contains one-fifth (1/5) oxygen.
  • John Dalton (1766–1844) presented the atomic theory of matter.
  • Avogadro (1776–1856) presented Avogadro's law about the number of molecules in gases.
  • J.J. Berzelius (1779–1848) introduced chemical symbols, formulas and chemical equations.
  • Mendeleev (1824–1907) discovered the periodic arrangement of the elements.

Importance of Chemistry in Daily Life

Chemistry serves every field of daily life: cooking and preserving food, medicines, cleaning products, fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture, fuels, clothes, plastics and paints. Every everyday thing is made of atoms and molecules, and its properties depend on its chemical composition; for example food, water and medicines are all chemical substances.

mcqs.q: Who first presented the idea that matter is made of a smallest indivisible particle (the atom)?
mcqs.why: Democritus (460–357 BC) presented the idea that matter is made of a smallest indivisible particle, which was named the atom. Aristotle and Plato gave other ideas about matter.

mcqs.q: Who gave the idea of the four elements — fire, water, earth and air?
mcqs.why: Aristotle presented the theory of the form of matter and gave the idea of four elements: fire, water, earth and air. This idea remained popular for a long time.

mcqs.q: Who invented the experimental methods for preparing nitric acid and hydrochloric acid?
mcqs.why: Jabir bin Hayyan (721–803 AD) invented experimental methods for nitric acid and hydrochloric acid and also described methods of dyeing cloth.

mcqs.q: Who prepared ethyl alcohol?
mcqs.why: Al-Razi prepared ethyl alcohol by the fermentation method. He was a famous Muslim scientist of the period 862–930 AD.

mcqs.q: Who determined the densities of different substances?
mcqs.why: Al-Beruni (973–1048 AD) determined the densities of different substances. Ibn Sina worked in medicine, philosophy and astronomy.

mcqs.q: Who discovered hydrogen gas?
mcqs.why: Cavendish (1731–1810) discovered hydrogen gas. Priestley discovered oxygen, while Scheele discovered chlorine gas.

mcqs.q: Who discovered that air contains one-fifth oxygen?
mcqs.why: Lavoisier (1743–1794) discovered that air contains one-fifth (1/5) oxygen. He is remembered for careful experiments on gases and burning.

mcqs.q: Who presented the atomic theory of matter?
mcqs.why: John Dalton (1766–1844) presented the atomic theory of matter. Mendeleev later arranged the elements in the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Who introduced chemical symbols, formulas and chemical equations?
mcqs.why: J.J. Berzelius (1779–1848) introduced chemical symbols, chemical formulas and chemical equations, and did research work in chemistry.

mcqs.q: Chemistry is useful in daily life for:
options: Food, medicines, fuels, clothes and plastics
mcqs.why: Chemistry serves every field of daily life: cooking and preserving food, medicines, cleaning products, fertilizers and pesticides, fuels, clothes, plastics and paints.

lessons.title: 1.2 Branches of Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
What are the Branches of Chemistry?

As knowledge of chemistry increased, it was divided into branches so that each part of the subject could be studied in detail. The main branches of chemistry are:

  • Physical chemistry: study of the physical properties, changes and energy of matter.
  • Organic chemistry: study of carbon compounds, especially the compounds of carbon and hydrogen (hydrocarbons).
  • Inorganic chemistry: study of compounds other than carbon compounds.
  • Analytical chemistry: study of the composition of matter — identifying its components and measuring their amounts.
  • Biochemistry: study of chemical processes in living things.

Physical Chemistry vs Analytical Chemistry

Physical chemistry studies the physical properties, changes and energy of matter, while analytical chemistry deals with identifying the composition of matter and measuring the amounts of its components.

Examples

  • Hydrocarbon compounds (carbon and hydrogen) belong to organic chemistry.
  • Glass, cement and metal-making are connected with industrial applications of chemistry.
  • The study of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in living bodies belongs to biochemistry.

mcqs.q: Which branch deals with hydrocarbon compounds?
mcqs.why: Organic Chemistry deals with hydrocarbon compounds, because this branch studies the compounds of carbon and hydrogen.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between physical chemistry and analytical chemistry?
options: Physical chemistry studies composition; analytical studies energy
Physical chemistry studies physical properties, changes and energy of matter; analytical chemistry identifies composition and measures amounts
mcqs.why: Physical chemistry studies the physical properties, changes and energy of matter, while analytical chemistry deals with identifying the composition of matter and measuring the amounts of its components.

mcqs.q: The study of carbon compounds is called:
mcqs.why: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Inorganic chemistry studies compounds other than those of carbon.

mcqs.q: The branch that studies chemical processes in living things is:
mcqs.why: Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies the chemical processes taking place in living things, such as those of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

mcqs.q: Analytical chemistry deals with:
options: Identifying the composition of matter and measuring the amounts of its components
mcqs.why: Analytical chemistry deals with identifying what a substance is made of (composition) and measuring how much of each component is present.

mcqs.q: Glass, cement and metal industries are applications of which side of chemistry?
mcqs.why: The making of glass, cement and metals on a large scale belongs to industrial chemistry, which applies chemical knowledge in industries.

mcqs.q: Which branch studies the physical properties and energy changes of matter?
mcqs.why: Physical chemistry studies the physical properties, changes and energy of matter, such as what happens during melting, boiling and chemical reactions.

mcqs.q: The study of compounds other than carbon compounds is:
mcqs.why: Inorganic chemistry is the study of compounds other than carbon compounds, for example salts, acids, bases and metals.

mcqs.q: Measuring how much of each component is present in a sample is the work of:
mcqs.why: Analytical chemistry measures the amounts of the components of matter, along with identifying the composition of the substance.

mcqs.q: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the living body are studied in:
mcqs.why: Biochemistry studies the chemical processes in living things, which include carbohydrates, proteins and fats present in living bodies.

lessons.title: 1.3 Basic Definitions
lessons.notes_html:
Matter and Substance

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space (volume). A chemical substance is the pure form of matter with fixed composition and fixed properties, such as an element or a compound.

Element, Compound and Mixture

  • Element: a substance made of only one kind of atom, e.g. hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Compound: a substance in which elements are joined by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio; its properties are different from its components, e.g. water.
  • Mixture: a substance in which components are physically mixed in any ratio; it can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation and distillation, e.g. ice cream and blood.

Important Definitions

  • Gram atomic mass: the mass of one mole of atoms of an element in grams.
  • Gram molecular mass: the mass of one mole of molecules of a substance in grams.
  • Gram formula mass: the mass of one mole of formula units of an ionic compound in grams.
  • Atomic mass in grams: when the atomic mass of an element is expressed in grams it is called gram atomic mass.

Chemical, Empirical and Molecular Formulas

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms in a molecule.

Formula: Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

SubstanceChemical FormulaEmpirical FormulaMolecular Formula
Sulphuric acidH2SO4H2SO4H2SO4
Carbon dioxideCO2CO2CO2
GlucoseC6H12O6CH2OC6H12O6
BenzeneC6H6CHC6H6

For glucose, the empirical formula is CH2O and n = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6. The empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is HO, because the simplest ratio of H to O is 1:1.

Identifying Elements, Compounds and Mixtures

  • Table salt: compound. Ice cream: mixture. Blood: mixture. Silicon: element. Coca-Cola: mixture. Tin: element. Zinc: element. Sulphur in water: mixture.
  • Elements present — washing soda (Na2CO3): sodium, carbon, oxygen. Sugar (C12H22O11): carbon, hydrogen, oxygen. Sand (SiO2): silicon, oxygen. Caustic soda (NaOH): sodium, oxygen, hydrogen.

mcqs.q: What is the atomic mass of an element expressed in grams called?
mcqs.why: It is called gram atomic mass, i.e. the mass of one mole of atoms of the element expressed in grams.

mcqs.q: Which of the following can be separated by a physical method?
mcqs.why: A mixture can be separated by a physical method, because its components can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation and distillation.

mcqs.q: Which formula shows the actual number of atoms in a molecule?
mcqs.why: The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms in a molecule, such as C6H12O6 for glucose. The empirical formula shows only the simplest ratio.

mcqs.q: What is the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)?
mcqs.why: The empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide is HO, because in H2O2 the simplest whole-number ratio of H to O is 1:1.

mcqs.q: What is the pure form of matter called?
mcqs.why: The pure form of matter is called a substance, i.e. the form of matter which has fixed composition and fixed properties.

mcqs.q: The mass of one mole of molecules of a substance in grams is called:
mcqs.why: Gram molecular mass is the mass of one mole of molecules of a substance in grams. For atoms it is gram atomic mass, and for ionic formula units it is gram formula mass.

mcqs.q: Gram formula mass is the mass of one mole of:
options: Formula units of an ionic compound
mcqs.why: Gram formula mass is the mass of one mole of formula units of an ionic compound in grams, used for ionic compounds which do not form separate molecules.

mcqs.q: Why are hydrogen and oxygen elements but water is not?
options: Hydrogen and oxygen each consist of one kind of atom; water is a compound of them in a fixed ratio
mcqs.why: Hydrogen and oxygen each consist of only one kind of atom, so they are elements. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen joined chemically in a fixed ratio, and its properties are quite different from those of its components.

mcqs.q: The empirical formula of glucose is CH2O and its molecular mass gives n = 6. Its molecular formula is:
mcqs.why: Molecular formula = n × empirical formula = 6 × CH2O = C6H12O6. So the molecular formula of glucose is C6H12O6.

mcqs.q: The relation between molecular formula and empirical formula is:
mcqs.why: Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass, and n is a whole number.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a mixture?
mcqs.why: Ice cream is a mixture because its components are physically mixed in no fixed ratio. Table salt is a compound, while silicon and tin are elements.

mcqs.q: Blood is classified as:
mcqs.why: Blood is a mixture, because many components are physically mixed in it in no fixed ratio and it has no fixed composition.

mcqs.q: The elements present in washing soda (Na2CO3) are:
mcqs.why: Washing soda has the formula Na2CO3, so the elements present in it are sodium, carbon and oxygen.

mcqs.q: The empirical formula of benzene (C6H6) is:
mcqs.why: In benzene C6H6, the simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen is 1:1, so its empirical formula is CH.

mcqs.q: Matter is anything that:
mcqs.why: Matter is anything that has mass and volume (occupies space). A chemical substance is the pure form of matter with fixed composition and properties.

lessons.title: 1.4 Chemical Species
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Chemical Species?

A chemical species is a basic particle taking part in a chemical process. The main chemical species are atom, molecule, ion and free radical.

  • Atom: the smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction; it is neutral.
  • Molecule: a neutral group of two or more atoms joined together.
  • Ion: a charged atom or group of atoms, formed by gaining or losing electrons; positive (cation) or negative (anion).
  • Free radical: an atom or group having one unpaired electron, such as Cl• and CH3•. It is very reactive.

Types of Molecules (by number of atoms)

  • Monoatomic molecule: one atom, e.g. He, Ne.
  • Diatomic molecule: two atoms, e.g. H2, O2, Cl2.
  • Triatomic molecule: three atoms, e.g. H2O, CO2.
  • Polyatomic molecule: many atoms, e.g. H2SO4, C6H12O6.

Homoatomic and Heteroatomic Molecules

A molecule whose atoms are all of the same element is homoatomic, e.g. H2. A molecule containing atoms of different elements is heteroatomic.

Atom vs Ion; Molecule vs Molecular Ion; Compound vs Mixture

  • An atom is neutral; an ion carries a positive or negative charge.
  • A molecule is a neutral group of atoms; a molecular ion is a charged group such as NH4+ and SO4--.
  • In a compound the components are joined by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio; in a mixture the components are physically mixed in any ratio.

mcqs.q: What is a molecule containing two atoms called?
mcqs.why: A molecule containing two atoms is called a diatomic molecule, such as H2, O2 and Cl2. A one-atom molecule is monoatomic.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a homoatomic molecule?
mcqs.why: H2 is a homoatomic molecule because both its atoms belong to the same element (hydrogen). NH3, H2O and CO2 contain atoms of different elements.

mcqs.q: What is a free radical?
options: An atom or group having one unpaired electron
mcqs.why: A free radical is an atom or group having one unpaired electron, such as Cl• and CH3•. Because of the unpaired electron, it is very reactive.

mcqs.q: A chemical species is:
options: A basic particle taking part in a chemical process
mcqs.why: A chemical species is a basic particle taking part in a chemical process. Atom, molecule, ion and free radical are all chemical species.

mcqs.q: An ion differs from an atom because an ion:
options: Carries a positive or negative charge
mcqs.why: An atom is neutral, while an ion carries a positive or negative charge because it is formed by gaining or losing electrons.

mcqs.q: NH4+ and SO4-- are examples of:
mcqs.why: NH4+ and SO4-- are molecular ions — charged groups of atoms. A molecule is a neutral group, while a molecular ion carries a charge.

mcqs.q: He and Ne are examples of:
mcqs.why: Helium and neon exist as single atoms, so they are monoatomic molecules. H2 is diatomic and H2SO4 is polyatomic.

mcqs.q: H2O and CO2 are:
mcqs.why: H2O and CO2 each contain three atoms, so they are triatomic molecules. Molecules with many atoms, like H2SO4, are polyatomic.

mcqs.q: In a compound, the components are:
options: Joined by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio
mcqs.why: In a compound the components are joined by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio, while in a mixture the components are physically mixed in any ratio.

mcqs.q: Why is a free radical very reactive?
options: It has a full outer shell
mcqs.why: A free radical has one unpaired electron, such as Cl• and CH3•, and it tries to pair this electron, so it is very reactive.

lessons.title: 1.5 Chemical Equations and Balancing Chemical Equations
lessons.notes_html:
Chemical Equations

A chemical equation shows a chemical reaction with the help of symbols and formulas. The substances on the left side are reactants and those on the right side are products.

Steps of Balancing an Equation

  • First: write the unbalanced (skeleton) equation.
  • Second: count the atoms of each element on both sides.
  • Third: equalise the numbers of atoms with coefficients, but never change the subscripts.
  • Fourth: re-count at the end to check.

Worked Examples

  • 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O
  • 2KNO3 → 2KNO2 + O2
  • Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2
  • 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2
  • 2CO + O2 → 2CO2
  • CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2
  • 4KClO3 → 4KCl + 6O2 (both sides have 4 K, 4 Cl and 12 O atoms)

mcqs.q: What is the first step of balancing a chemical equation?
mcqs.why: The first step is to write the unbalanced (skeleton) equation. Then the atoms of each element are counted on both sides.

mcqs.q: While balancing an equation, what must never be changed?
mcqs.why: The numbers of atoms are equalised with coefficients, but the subscripts of the formulas must never be changed, because changing a subscript changes the substance itself.

mcqs.q: The balanced equation for NH3 + O2 → NO + H2O is:
mcqs.why: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O is balanced: both sides have 4 N, 12 H and 10 O atoms.

mcqs.q: KNO3 → KNO2 + O2 is balanced as:
mcqs.why: 2KNO3 → 2KNO2 + O2 is balanced: both sides have 2 K, 2 N and 6 O atoms.

mcqs.q: Ca + H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2 is balanced as:
mcqs.why: Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2 is balanced: both sides have 1 Ca, 4 H and 2 O atoms.

mcqs.q: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 — this equation is:
mcqs.why: It is balanced: both sides have 2 Na, 2 H, 2 C and 6 O atoms, so the numbers of atoms are equal on the two sides.

mcqs.q: CO + O2 → CO2 is balanced as:
mcqs.why: 2CO + O2 → 2CO2 is balanced: both sides have 2 C and 4 O atoms.

mcqs.q: CaCO3 + HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2 is balanced as:
mcqs.why: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2 is balanced: both sides have 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H and 2 Cl atoms.

mcqs.q: In 4KClO3 → 4KCl + 6O2, the number of oxygen atoms on each side is:
mcqs.why: On the left side 4 × 3 = 12 oxygen atoms, and on the right side 6 × 2 = 12 oxygen atoms, so the equation is balanced for oxygen.

mcqs.q: The last step of balancing an equation is:
options: To re-count the atoms at the end to check
mcqs.why: After placing coefficients, the atoms of every element are re-counted at the end to check that both sides are equal.

lessons.title: 1.6 Mole and Avogadro's Number
lessons.notes_html:
The Mole

A mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles.

Avogadro's Number

The number 6.02 × 10^23 is called Avogadro's number (NA). One mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number of particles, so the mole and Avogadro's number are directly linked.

Molar Mass

The mass of one mole of a substance is its molar mass. For example, the molecular mass of H2SO4 is 98 a.m.u, so its molar mass is 98 g — one mole of H2SO4 weighs 98 gram.

Formula: Number of moles = given mass ÷ molar mass

mcqs.q: What is the molar mass of H2SO4?
mcqs.why: The molar mass of H2SO4 is 98 gram, because the molecular mass of H2SO4 is 98 a.m.u, so one mole weighs 98 gram.

mcqs.q: One mole of any substance contains how many particles?
mcqs.why: One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles, and this number is called Avogadro's number (NA).

mcqs.q: Avogadro's number is:
options: The number of atoms in hydrogen
The number of particles in one mole, 6.02 × 10^23
mcqs.why: Avogadro's number (NA) is 6.02 × 10^23, the number of particles (atoms, molecules or ions) present in one mole of a substance.

mcqs.q: The mole is related to Avogadro's number because:
options: One mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number of particles
mcqs.why: One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles, and this very number is called Avogadro's number, so the mole and Avogadro's number are linked.

mcqs.q: The molar mass of a substance is numerically equal to its:
options: Molecular or formula mass in a.m.u, expressed in grams
mcqs.why: The molar mass is the mass of one mole. For H2SO4 the molecular mass is 98 a.m.u, so the molar mass is 98 g per mole.

mcqs.q: The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10^23 particles is called:
mcqs.why: One mole of a substance contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles. This counting unit is used for atoms, molecules and ions.

mcqs.q: One mole of H2SO4 weighs:
mcqs.why: The molecular mass of H2SO4 is 98 a.m.u, so one mole of H2SO4 weighs 98 gram.

mcqs.q: Which quantity is the same for one mole of every substance?
mcqs.why: One mole of every substance contains the same number of particles, 6.02 × 10^23, although the masses of one mole are different.

mcqs.q: The number of moles in a given mass is found by:
mcqs.why: Number of moles = given mass ÷ molar mass. For example, the moles in 40 g of H2SO4 are 40 ÷ 98 = 0.41 mol.

mcqs.q: Avogadro's number is represented by the symbol:
mcqs.why: Avogadro's number is represented by NA and its value is 6.02 × 10^23 particles per mole.

lessons.title: 1.7 Stoichiometry (Chemical Calculations)
lessons.notes_html:
Formula Mass and Molecular Mass

Formula mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a formula unit. Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.

Worked Examples — Formula Mass

  • Al2O3 = 2 × 27 + 3 × 16 = 54 + 48 = 102 a.m.u
  • MgCl2 = 24 + 2 × 35.5 = 24 + 71 = 95 a.m.u
  • NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 a.m.u
  • KNO3 = 39 + 14 + 3 × 16 = 39 + 14 + 48 = 101 a.m.u

Worked Examples — Molecular Mass

  • C2H5OH = 2 × 12 + 6 × 1 + 16 = 24 + 6 + 16 = 46 a.m.u
  • H2O = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 a.m.u
  • NH3 = 14 + 3 × 1 = 17 a.m.u
  • CO2 = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 a.m.u

Calculating Moles and Molecules — Full Steps

Example 1: How many moles are needed to get 40 g of H2SO4?

Molar mass of H2SO4 = 98 g

Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass = 40 ÷ 98 = 0.41 mol

Example 2: Moles and molecules in 16 g of H2CO3:

Molar mass of H2CO3 = 62 g

Moles = 16 ÷ 62 = 0.26 mol

Molecules = 0.26 × 6.02 × 10^23 = 1.56 × 10^23

Example 3: Moles and molecules in 20 g of C6H12O6:

Molar mass of C6H12O6 = 180 g

Moles = 20 ÷ 180 = 0.11 mol

Molecules = 0.11 × 6.02 × 10^23 = 6.7 × 10^22

Example 4: Moles in 30 g of H3PO4:

Molar mass of H3PO4 = 3 × 1 + 31 + 4 × 16 = 98 g

Moles = 30 ÷ 98 = 0.31 mol

Formulas: Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass; Number of particles = moles × 6.02 × 10^23

mcqs.q: The formula mass of Al2O3 is:
mcqs.why: Al2O3 = 2 × 27 + 3 × 16 = 54 + 48 = 102 a.m.u. The atomic masses used are Al = 27 and O = 16.

mcqs.q: The formula mass of MgCl2 is:
The formula mass of NaCl is:
mcqs.why: NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 a.m.u, using Na = 23 and Cl = 35.5.

mcqs.q: The molecular mass of C2H5OH is:
The molecular mass of NH3 is:
mcqs.why: NH3 = 14 + 3 × 1 = 17 a.m.u, using N = 14 and H = 1.

mcqs.q: How many moles are needed to get 40 g of H2SO4 (molar mass 98 g)?
mcqs.why: Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass = 40 ÷ 98 = 0.41 mol. This is the basic stoichiometry formula.

mcqs.q: The number of moles in 16 g of H2CO3 (molar mass 62 g) is:
mcqs.why: Moles = 16 ÷ 62 = 0.26 mol, and the number of molecules = 0.26 × 6.02 × 10^23 = 1.56 × 10^23.

mcqs.q: The number of molecules in 20 g of C6H12O6 (molar mass 180 g) is:
The number of moles in 30 g of H3PO4 (molar mass 98 g) is:
mcqs.why: Molar mass of H3PO4 = 3 × 1 + 31 + 4 × 16 = 98 g. Moles = 30 ÷ 98 = 0.31 mol.

lessons.title: 2.1 Discovery of Subatomic Particles: Electron, Proton and Neutron
lessons.notes_html:
Subatomic Particles

The atom is made of three fundamental subatomic particles: electron, proton and neutron. Protons and neutrons are present in the nucleus, while electrons revolve around the nucleus.

ParticleMassCharge
Proton1.67 × 10^-27 kg+1
Neutron1.67 × 10^-27 kg0 (no charge)
Electron9.1 × 10^-31 kg−1

Atomic Number and Mass Number

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons in the atom. For example, an oxygen atom has 8 protons, so its atomic number is 8.
  • Mass number (A), also called nucleon number, = total number of protons and neutrons. For example, a chlorine atom with 17 protons and 18 neutrons has mass number 17 + 18 = 35.
  • Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • The mass of the atom is shown by the protons and neutrons, which are in the nucleus and make up almost all the mass of the atom.
  • The hydrogen atom (protium, 1H) has no neutron.

Discovery of the Electron — Cathode Rays

Cathode rays are obtained by passing electricity through a gas at low pressure and high voltage in a discharge tube. Their properties are:

  • They travel in straight lines.
  • They carry negative charge.
  • They bend in electric and magnetic fields.
  • They can pass through metal foil.

Experiments Proving Electrons, Protons and Neutrons

  • Electron: the cathode-ray experiment (Crookes and Thomson).
  • Proton: Goldstein's canal-ray experiment.
  • Neutron: Chadwick's experiment, in which alpha particles were fired at beryllium and chargeless particles came out.

Worked Example

In 59Co27: protons = 27, electrons = 27, neutrons = 59 − 27 = 32.

mcqs.q: What is the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom called?
mcqs.why: The total number of protons and neutrons is called the nucleon number, also known as the mass number (A). The atomic number is only the number of protons.

mcqs.q: Which particle inside the nucleus has no charge?
mcqs.why: The neutron carries no charge. The proton carries a +1 charge and the electron a −1 charge.

mcqs.q: Cathode rays are obtained by passing electricity through a gas at:
mcqs.why: Cathode rays are obtained by passing electricity through a gas at low pressure and high voltage in a discharge tube, as in the experiments of Crookes and Thomson.

mcqs.q: Which property shows that cathode rays carry negative charge?
options: They bend in electric and magnetic fields
mcqs.why: Cathode rays bend in electric and magnetic fields, which shows they are made of negatively charged particles — the electrons.

mcqs.q: The neutron was discovered by Chadwick in an experiment in which alpha particles were fired at:
mcqs.why: Chadwick fired alpha particles at beryllium and chargeless particles came out; these were named neutrons.

mcqs.q: The proton was discovered through:
mcqs.why: The proton was found through Goldstein's canal-ray experiment. The electron came from the cathode-ray experiment and the neutron from Chadwick's experiment.

mcqs.q: The mass of a proton is:
mcqs.why: The mass of a proton is 1.67 × 10^-27 kg with charge +1. The electron is much lighter, with mass 9.1 × 10^-31 kg and charge −1.

mcqs.q: An oxygen atom has 8 protons and 8 electrons. Its atomic number is:
mcqs.why: Atomic number = number of protons = 8. The number of electrons in a neutral atom is equal to the number of protons.

mcqs.q: A chlorine atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is:
mcqs.why: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35. The mass number counts all the nucleons in the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Which element's atom has no neutron?
mcqs.why: The hydrogen atom (protium, 1H) has no neutron; it has only one proton and one electron. Its other isotopes do have neutrons.

lessons.title: 2.2 Theories and Experiments Related to Structure of Atom
lessons.notes_html:
Rutherford's Gold-Foil Experiment

Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. The alpha particles struck a screen coated with zinc sulphide (ZnS) and produced flashes. The observations were:

  • Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
  • Some were deflected from their path.
  • A few bounced back.

Rutherford's Atomic Model

  • The atom is mostly empty space.
  • The positive charge and almost all the mass are gathered in a tiny central part called the nucleus.
  • Electrons revolve around the nucleus.
  • This model is based on the classical idea: electrons can revolve in any orbit.

Defects of Rutherford's Model

  • It could not explain how the positive charge stays together in the nucleus.
  • Orbiting electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus, yet the atom is stable.
  • It could not explain the line spectrum of the atom.

Bohr's Model vs Rutherford's Model

According to Rutherford, electrons can revolve in any orbit, whereas according to Bohr, electrons revolve only in fixed-energy orbits and absorb or release energy when changing orbit. Bohr's model is based on the quantum idea; Rutherford's on the classical idea. In Bohr's model, electrons take in or give out packets (quanta) of energy when they change orbit.

mcqs.q: What material was used for the screen in Rutherford's atomic model experiment?
mcqs.why: Zinc sulphide (ZnS) was used on the screen; the alpha particles struck it and produced flashes, so their positions could be observed.

mcqs.q: In Rutherford's gold-foil experiment, most alpha particles:
mcqs.why: Most alpha particles passed straight through, which showed that the atom is mostly empty space. Only a few were deflected or bounced back.

mcqs.q: The conclusion that the positive charge and mass are gathered in a tiny nucleus came from:
options: A few alpha particles bouncing back in the gold-foil experiment
mcqs.why: A few alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil, showing that the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

mcqs.q: Which is a defect of Rutherford's atomic model?
options: Orbiting electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus, yet the atom is stable
mcqs.why: According to classical theory, orbiting electrons should continuously lose energy and fall into the nucleus, but atoms are stable. Rutherford's model could not explain this, nor the line spectrum.

mcqs.q: Rutherford's model could not explain:
options: The line spectrum of the atom
mcqs.why: Rutherford's model could not explain the line spectrum of the atom, nor how the positive charge stays together in the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Bohr's model differs from Rutherford's model because in Bohr's model electrons:
mcqs.why: According to Bohr, electrons revolve only in fixed-energy orbits and absorb or release energy when changing orbit. Rutherford allowed electrons in any orbit.

mcqs.q: Rutherford's model is based on the classical idea, while Bohr's model is based on:
mcqs.why: Bohr's model is based on the quantum idea: electrons revolve in fixed-energy orbits and take in or give out packets (quanta) of energy.

mcqs.q: In the gold-foil experiment, the particles fired at the foil were:
mcqs.why: Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil and observed their scattering on a zinc sulphide screen.

mcqs.q: According to Rutherford's model, electrons:
mcqs.why: In Rutherford's model, electrons revolve around the tiny, positively charged nucleus, and the atom is mostly empty space.

mcqs.q: When an electron changes orbit in Bohr's model, it:
mcqs.why: In Bohr's model, an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit and releases energy when it falls to a lower orbit.

lessons.title: 2.3 Modern Theories of Structure of Atom
lessons.notes_html:
De Broglie's Hypothesis

In 1923, de Broglie presented the hypothesis that every moving particle also has wave-like properties. The electron too behaves like a wave, so the electron has a dual (wave-particle) nature.

Formula: λ = h/mv, where h is Planck's constant, m is mass and v is velocity of the particle.

Proof of De Broglie's Relation

Planck's equation: E = hν and Einstein's equation: E = mc². Equating them gives hν = mc². Putting ν = c/λ gives h/λ = mc, so λ = h/mc. For a moving particle, λ = h/mv, which is de Broglie's equation.

Defects of Bohr's Atomic Model

  • It applies only to single-electron particles (like hydrogen).
  • It does not explain the fine structure of electron orbits (spectra).
  • It goes against Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, because the position and velocity of an electron cannot both be known at the same time.

Schrödinger's Atomic Model

According to Schrödinger, electrons are not in fixed orbits but in orbitals, where there is a probability of finding them. The structure of the atom is described by the wave equation. This model is based on quantum mechanics.

mcqs.q: In which year was de Broglie's hypothesis about the wave nature of the electron proposed?
mcqs.why: De Broglie's hypothesis about the wave nature of the electron was proposed in 1923. It says every moving particle has wave-like properties.

mcqs.q: De Broglie's hypothesis states that:
options: Every moving particle also has wave-like properties
mcqs.why: De Broglie stated that every moving particle also has wave-like properties; the electron too behaves like a wave, so it has a dual nature.

mcqs.q: The de Broglie wavelength is given by:
mcqs.why: λ = h/mv, where h is Planck's constant, m is the mass of the particle and v is its velocity.

mcqs.q: In λ = h/mv, h is:
mcqs.why: In de Broglie's equation, h is Planck's constant, m is mass and v is velocity of the moving particle.

mcqs.q: Which is a defect of Bohr's atomic model?
options: It applies only to single-electron particles
mcqs.why: Bohr's model applies only to single-electron particles like hydrogen. It also does not explain the fine structure of spectra.

mcqs.q: Bohr's model goes against Heisenberg's uncertainty principle because:
options: The position and velocity of an electron cannot both be known at the same time
mcqs.why: Bohr's model fixes both the orbit (position) and speed of the electron, but Heisenberg's principle says the position and velocity of an electron cannot both be known exactly at the same time.

mcqs.q: According to Schrödinger's model, electrons are found in:
options: Orbitals, where there is a probability of finding them
mcqs.why: Schrödinger's model places electrons in orbitals — regions where there is a probability of finding them — instead of fixed orbits.

mcqs.q: Schrödinger's atomic model is based on:
options: Quantum mechanics and the wave equation
mcqs.why: Schrödinger described atomic structure by the wave equation, and his model is based on quantum mechanics.

mcqs.q: Combining Planck's E = hν with Einstein's E = mc² gives de Broglie's relation. Here ν = c/λ is substituted to obtain:
mcqs.why: hν = mc² and ν = c/λ give h/λ = mc, so λ = h/mc. For a moving particle this becomes λ = h/mv, de Broglie's equation.

mcqs.q: The dual nature of the electron means the electron behaves as:
options: Both a particle and a wave
mcqs.why: The electron shows both particle and wave properties. This wave-particle duality is the basis of de Broglie's hypothesis.

lessons.title: 2.4 Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
Shells and Subshells

  • A shell is the main energy level of electrons in an atom: K, L, M, N.
  • A subshell is a smaller division of a shell: s, p, d, f. Example: the L shell contains the 2s and 2p subshells.
  • An s subshell can hold a maximum of 2 electrons.
  • The arrangement (configuration) of electrons belongs to the electron, because electrons are arranged in shells and subshells.
  • Electrons fill shells in order because inner shells have lower energy, so electrons first fill the lower-energy shells.

Working Out Configurations

  • If the K and L shells are completely full, the atom has 2 + 8 = 10 electrons in total.
  • Potassium (19 electrons): 2, 8, 8, 1.
  • Sodium (Z = 11): 2, 8, 1 — so its L shell has 8 electrons.

Worked Example — Atom with 5 Electrons in the M Shell

(a) Atomic number = 2 + 8 + 5 = 15

(b) Electronic configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, or 2, 8, 5

(c) Element: phosphorus (P)

Counting Protons, Neutrons and Electrons

AtomProtonsElectronsNeutrons
56Fe26262630
17O8889
37Cl17171720
235U929292143
14C6668

Potassium has nucleon number 39 and proton number 19, so its neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20.

mcqs.q: Potassium has proton number 19. What is its electron arrangement?
mcqs.why: Potassium has 19 electrons, distributed as 2, 8, 8, 1 in the K, L, M and N shells.

mcqs.q: Potassium has nucleon number 39. How many neutrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Neutrons = mass number − proton number = 39 − 19 = 20.

mcqs.q: The arrangement of electrons in shells and subshells belongs to which particle?
mcqs.why: It is the electrons that are arranged in shells and subshells; protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus.

mcqs.q: How many subshells are there in the L shell?
mcqs.why: The L shell has two subshells, namely 2s and 2p. The K shell has only one subshell (1s).

mcqs.q: An atom has 5 electrons in its M shell. The element is:
mcqs.why: Atomic number = 2 + 8 + 5 = 15, with configuration 2, 8, 5 (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³). Element 15 is phosphorus (P).

mcqs.q: How many electrons can an s subshell hold at most?
mcqs.why: An s subshell can hold a maximum of 2 electrons. A p subshell can hold 6 and a d subshell 10.

mcqs.q: An atom with atomic number 11 (sodium) has how many electrons in its L shell?
mcqs.why: Sodium (Z = 11) has the arrangement 2, 8, 1, so there are 8 electrons in the L shell and 1 in the M shell.

mcqs.q: Why do electrons fill shells in order?
options: Inner shells have lower energy, so they fill first
mcqs.why: Inner shells have lower energy, so electrons first fill the lower-energy shells and then move to higher shells.

mcqs.q: If the K and L shells of an atom are completely full, the total number of electrons is:
mcqs.why: The K shell holds 2 and the L shell holds 8 electrons, so a completely full K and L means 2 + 8 = 10 electrons in total.

mcqs.q: In 56Fe26, the number of neutrons is:
mcqs.why: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 56 − 26 = 30. Iron-56 has 26 protons, 26 electrons and 30 neutrons.

lessons.title: 2.5 Isotopes and Their Common Uses
lessons.notes_html:
What are Isotopes?

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different nucleon numbers, i.e. they differ in the number of neutrons.

Isotopes of Chlorine

  • 35Cl17: 17 protons, 18 neutrons.
  • 37Cl17: 17 protons, 20 neutrons.

Isotopes of Hydrogen

  • Protium: 1 proton, 0 neutrons.
  • Deuterium: 1 proton, 1 neutron.
  • Tritium: 1 proton, 2 neutrons.

Isotopes of Carbon and Oxygen

All isotopes of carbon have 6 protons, with 6, 7 or 8 neutrons. The abundance of the carbon-12 isotope is about 98.9%. 16O and 17O are alike because both have 8 protons and 8 electrons and the same chemical properties; they differ because 16O has 8 neutrons and 17O has 9 neutrons, so their masses and physical properties differ.

Why Same Chemical but Different Physical Properties?

Chemical properties depend on the electron arrangement, which is the same in isotopes, while physical properties depend on the mass number, which differs.

Uses of Isotopes in Daily Life

  • Carbon-14 is used to date old objects.
  • Cobalt-60 is used in cancer treatment; its gamma rays also sterilise medical instruments because they carry very high energy and kill germs.
  • Iodine-131 is used to examine thyroid disease.
  • Uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear power stations.

mcqs.q: What is the abundance of the carbon-12 isotope (as given in the book's options)?
mcqs.why: The abundance of carbon-12 is 98.89% according to the book's question options (the chapter text gives about 98.9%). Carbon-12 is the most common isotope of carbon.

mcqs.q: Which rays are used to sterilise medical instruments?
mcqs.why: Gamma rays are used to sterilise medical instruments because they carry very high energy and kill germs. Cobalt-60 is a source of gamma rays.

mcqs.q: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with:
options: Same proton number but different nucleon numbers
mcqs.why: Isotopes have the same proton number but different nucleon numbers, because the number of neutrons differs, e.g. 35Cl17 and 37Cl17.

mcqs.q: The isotopes of chlorine, 35Cl17 and 37Cl17, contain neutrons respectively:
mcqs.why: 35Cl17 has 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons, and 37Cl17 has 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons. Both have the same 17 protons.

mcqs.q: Carbon-14 is used for:
mcqs.why: Carbon-14 is used to date old objects (radiocarbon dating). Cobalt-60 is used in cancer treatment and uranium-235 as nuclear fuel.

mcqs.q: Iodine-131 is used to examine disease of the:
mcqs.why: Iodine-131 is used to examine thyroid disease, because iodine collects in the thyroid gland of the body.

mcqs.q: Uranium-235 is used as:
mcqs.why: Uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear power stations. Other isotopes serve in medicine and research.

mcqs.q: 16O and 17O have the same chemical properties because both have:
mcqs.why: Both have 8 protons and 8 electrons, so their electron arrangement and chemical properties are the same; they differ in neutrons (8 and 9) and hence in mass.

mcqs.q: Isotopes have different physical properties because physical properties depend on:
mcqs.why: Physical properties depend on the mass number, which differs in isotopes because the number of neutrons differs, while chemical properties depend on electron arrangement.

mcqs.q: How many neutrons are in tritium, the isotope of hydrogen?
mcqs.why: Tritium has 1 proton and 2 neutrons. Protium has 0 neutrons and deuterium has 1 neutron.

chapters.title: 3. Periodic Table and Periodicity of Properties

lessons.title: 3.1 Periodic Table
lessons.notes_html:
What is the Periodic Table?

The periodic table is an ordered list of the elements in which the elements are arranged in increasing atomic number. It has 7 periods (horizontal rows) and 18 groups (vertical columns).

Early Attempts and Mendeleev's Periodic Law (1869)

Mendeleev presented the periodic law that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic mass. He arranged the elements in increasing order of atomic mass and grouped elements of similar properties together. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, which later proved correct. Lothar Meyer also presented a similar table of 56 elements in 1869.

Modern Periodic Law — Moseley (1913)

Moseley discovered that the atomic number is the basic property of an element. According to the modern periodic law, the chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number. The atomic number fixes the element's place in the table, its electronic configuration and its properties — so the periodic properties of an element depend on the number of protons in its atom.

Periods and Groups

  • A period is a horizontal row of the periodic table in which elements are in increasing atomic number.
  • A group is a vertical column whose elements have equal electrons in the outer shell and similar properties.
  • The 4th and 5th periods are called long periods because they contain 18 elements each.

Blocks of the Periodic Table

The table is divided into s, p, d and f blocks on the basis of electronic configuration, i.e. which subshell the last electron enters:

BlockGroupsLast electron enters
s blockIA and IIAs subshell
p blockIIIA to VIIIAp subshell
d blockTransition elementsd subshell
f blockLanthanides and actinidesf subshell

Families of Elements

  • Group IA: alkali metals (Li, Na, K).
  • Group IIA: alkaline-earth metals (Mg, Ca, Ba).
  • Groups IIIA to VIA: representative elements.
  • Group VIIA: halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) — fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
  • Group VIIIA: noble (inert) gases.
  • Groups IB to VIIIB: transition metals — the transition and inner-transition elements are metals, such as iron, copper and zinc.
  • Lanthanides: from lanthanum (La) to lutetium (Lu). Actinides: from actinium (Ac) to lawrencium (Lr).

Reading the Table

  • The atomic number is written at the top of each element's cell; for example carbon has atomic number 6 and sodium 11.
  • Each cell carries the element's symbol and name; for example H is hydrogen, O is oxygen, Fe is iron and Au is gold.
  • Most metals are solids with high melting points, bromine is a liquid, and non-metals such as hydrogen and oxygen are gases.
  • Elements of the same group (family) have equal electrons in the outer shell, so their chemical properties are similar and their physical properties change in order; e.g. the alkali metals Li, Na, K are all soft and reactive.

Electronic Configurations (examples)

  • Na (Z = 11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ or 2, 8, 1
  • Ca (Z = 20): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² or 2, 8, 8, 2
  • F (Z = 9): 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ or 2, 7
  • Si (Z = 14): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p² or 2, 8, 4

mcqs.q: Mendeleev (1869) presented his periodic law that the properties of elements are a periodic function of:
mcqs.why: Mendeleev's periodic law says the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic mass, because he arranged the elements in increasing order of atomic mass.

mcqs.q: On what basis is the periodic table divided into s, p, d and f blocks?
mcqs.why: The blocks are based on electronic configuration — which subshell the differentiating (last) electron enters: s, p, d or f.

mcqs.q: What are the 4th and 5th periods called?
mcqs.why: The 4th and 5th periods are called long periods because they contain 18 elements each.

mcqs.q: What are the Group VIIA elements called?
mcqs.why: Group VIIA elements are called halogens, such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine. Group VIIIA elements are the noble gases.

mcqs.q: According to Moseley, the chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of:
mcqs.why: Moseley showed that the chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number, which is the basis of the modern periodic law.

mcqs.q: The transition and inner-transition elements are:
mcqs.why: The transition and inner-transition elements are metals, such as iron, copper and zinc.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a period and a group?
options: A period is a vertical column; a group is a row
A period is a horizontal row; a group is a vertical column of elements with equal outer-shell electrons
mcqs.why: A period is a horizontal row in which elements are in increasing atomic number. A group is a vertical column whose elements have equal electrons in the outer shell and similar properties.

mcqs.q: The periodic table has:
mcqs.why: The periodic table has 7 periods (horizontal rows) and 18 groups (vertical columns), with elements arranged in increasing atomic number.

mcqs.q: In the s block, the last electron enters the s subshell. The s block contains groups:
mcqs.why: The s block contains Groups IA and IIA. The p block has IIIA to VIIIA, the d block the transition elements and the f block the lanthanides and actinides.

mcqs.q: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for:
options: Undiscovered elements, and predicted their properties
mcqs.why: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, which later proved correct — a great success of his table.

mcqs.q: Elements of the same group have similar chemical properties because they have:
options: Equal electrons in the outer shell
mcqs.why: Elements of the same group have equal electrons in the outer shell, so their chemical properties are similar; e.g. the alkali metals Li, Na, K are all soft and reactive.

mcqs.q: The lanthanide series runs from:
mcqs.why: The lanthanides run from lanthanum (La) to lutetium (Lu). The actinides run from actinium (Ac) to lawrencium (Lr).

mcqs.q: Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature?
mcqs.why: Among the halogens, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.

mcqs.q: The atomic number of an element in the periodic table is written:
options: At the bottom of the cell
At the top of the element's cell
mcqs.why: The atomic number is written at the top of each element's cell; for example carbon has atomic number 6 and sodium 11.

mcqs.q: The electronic configuration of calcium (Z = 20) is:
mcqs.why: Calcium (Z = 20) has configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s², i.e. 2, 8, 8, 2. Sodium is 2, 8, 1 and silicon is 2, 8, 4.

lessons.title: 3.2 Periodicity of Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Periodic Properties

Properties that change in a regular way across a period and down a group are called periodic properties. The main ones are atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

Atomic Radius

  • Across a period (left to right), the atomic radius decreases, because the nuclear pull increases while the shells stay the same.
  • Down a group, the atomic radius increases, because new shells keep being added.

Shielding Effect

The shielding effect is that the inner electrons hide (block) the nuclear pull from the outer electrons, so the outer electrons feel less pull. The greater the shielding, the weaker the nuclear effect and the larger the atomic radius. Across a period the shielding effect decreases in effect, because the nuclear charge increases while the inner electrons stay the same.

Ionisation Energy, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

  • Ionisation energy: the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom. Helium has the highest ionisation energy, because its atom is the smallest and its electrons are held very tightly by the nucleus.
  • Electron affinity: the energy change when an electron is added to an atom. It decreases down a group because the atomic size increases, so the nuclear pull on the outer electron decreases.
  • Electronegativity: the attraction of an atom for a shared pair of electrons in a bond.

Trends in a Group and a Period

PropertyDown a groupAcross a period (left → right)
Atomic radiusIncreasesDecreases
Ionisation energyDecreasesIncreases
Electron affinityDecreasesIncreases
ElectronegativityDecreasesIncreases

Electronegativity examples: down a group it decreases (F = 4.0, Cl = 3.0, Br = 2.8); across a period it increases (Li = 1.0, C = 2.5, F = 4.0). Ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity all increase across a period because the nuclear pull increases and the atomic size decreases.

Note: magnesium (Mg), an alkaline-earth metal, forms a protective oxide coating on its surface, which protects the metal underneath.

mcqs.q: What decreases from left to right in a period?
mcqs.why: The atomic radius decreases across a period because the nuclear pull increases while the number of shells stays the same, so the electrons are pulled closer.

mcqs.q: How does the shielding effect change across a period?
options: Stays exactly the same in effect
mcqs.why: Across a period the shielding effect decreases (in effect), because the nuclear charge increases while the inner electrons stay the same, so the outer electrons feel a stronger pull.

mcqs.q: What is the attraction for a shared pair of electrons called?
mcqs.why: Electronegativity is the attraction of an atom for a shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine has the highest value, 4.0.

mcqs.q: Why does electron affinity decrease down a group?
mcqs.why: Electron affinity decreases down a group because the atomic size increases, so the nuclear pull on the incoming outer electron decreases.

mcqs.q: Down a group, the atomic radius:
mcqs.why: Down a group the atomic radius increases, because new shells keep being added to the atoms.

mcqs.q: The trend of electronegativity across a period from left to right is:
mcqs.why: Electronegativity increases across a period (Li = 1.0, C = 2.5, F = 4.0) because the nuclear pull increases and the atomic size decreases.

mcqs.q: Down a group, electronegativity:
mcqs.why: Electronegativity decreases down a group: F = 4.0, Cl = 3.0 and Br = 2.8, because the atomic size increases down the group.

mcqs.q: Which element has the highest ionisation energy and why?
options: Hydrogen, because it has one electron
Fluorine, because it is most electronegative
Caesium, because it is the largest
Helium, because its atom is smallest and electrons are held tightly
mcqs.why: Helium has the highest ionisation energy because its atom is the smallest and its electrons are held very tightly by the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The shielding effect is:
options: Inner electrons blocking the nuclear pull from the outer electrons
mcqs.why: In the shielding effect, the inner electrons block the nuclear pull from reaching the outer electrons fully, so the outer electrons feel less pull.

mcqs.q: The greater the shielding effect, the atomic radius is:
mcqs.why: Greater shielding weakens the nuclear pull on the outer electrons, so the atom spreads out more and the atomic radius is larger.

mcqs.q: Across a period, ionisation energy generally:
mcqs.why: Ionisation energy increases across a period because the nuclear pull increases and the atomic size decreases, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.

mcqs.q: Down a group, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity all:
mcqs.why: Down a group all three decrease, because the atomic size increases and the nuclear pull on the outer electrons becomes weaker.

mcqs.q: Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. These are:
mcqs.why: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are the halogens of Group VIIA; their states change from gas to liquid to solid down the group.

mcqs.q: Which alkaline-earth metal forms a protective oxide coating on its surface?
mcqs.why: Magnesium (Mg), an alkaline-earth metal of Group IIA, forms a protective oxide layer (coating) on its surface.

mcqs.q: Across a period, atomic radius decreases mainly because:
options: Nuclear charge increases while shells stay the same
mcqs.why: Across a period the number of shells stays the same but the nuclear charge increases, so the electrons are pulled closer and the atomic radius decreases.

lessons.title: 4.1 Why Do Atoms Form Chemical Bonds?
lessons.notes_html:
Why Do Atoms Combine?

Atoms form chemical bonds to gain stability. Elements gain stability by completing their outer shell — by giving, taking or sharing electrons. Metals give electrons; non-metals take or share electrons, so that the octet or duplet is completed.

Octet Rule and Duplet Rule

  • Octet rule: an atom tends to complete 8 electrons in its outer (valence) shell to become stable.
  • Duplet rule: small atoms such as hydrogen and helium tend to complete 2 electrons in their shell.

Why are Noble Gases Stable?

Noble gases have 8 electrons in their valence shell (2 in helium), so their shells are complete. Therefore they need neither to gain nor to lose electrons, they do not react with other elements, and they are stable. For the same reason, a helium atom does not gain electrons: its shell already has 2 electrons and its duplet is complete.

Valence Shell and Valence Electrons

The outer shell of an atom is its valence shell, and it can hold at most 8 electrons. The electrons in this shell are called valence electrons. They are important because they take part in bonding and chemical reactions. For example, magnesium has 2 electrons in its valence shell (2, 8, 2).

mcqs.q: An atom's tendency to complete 8 electrons in its outer shell is called:
mcqs.why: The octet rule is the tendency of an atom to complete 8 electrons in its outer shell. Small atoms like hydrogen follow the duplet rule (2 electrons).

mcqs.q: Why are noble gases stable? Their valence shell has:
mcqs.why: Noble gases have 8 electrons in the valence shell (2 in helium), so their shells are complete and they need neither gain nor lose electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the Duplet Rule?
options: Completing 8 electrons in the outer shell
Small atoms like hydrogen and helium completing 2 electrons in their shell
mcqs.why: The duplet rule applies to small atoms such as hydrogen and helium, which tend to complete 2 electrons in their shell, like helium.

mcqs.q: Elements gain stability by:
options: Completing their outer shell by giving, taking or sharing electrons
mcqs.why: Elements gain stability by completing their outer shell: metals give electrons, non-metals take or share electrons, so that the octet or duplet is completed.

mcqs.q: Why does a helium atom not gain electrons?
options: Its shell already has 2 electrons and its duplet is complete
mcqs.why: The helium shell already has 2 electrons and its duplet is complete, so it is stable and does not gain electrons.

mcqs.q: Why do noble gases not react with other elements?
options: Their outer shells are complete (octet or duplet), so they are stable
mcqs.why: The outer shells of noble gases are complete, so they are stable and do not need to gain, lose or share electrons; hence they do not react.

mcqs.q: Valence electrons are important because they:
options: Take part in bonding and chemical reactions
mcqs.why: Valence electrons are the electrons of the outer shell; they take part in bonding and chemical reactions, so they decide the chemical behaviour of the element.

mcqs.q: A valence shell can hold at most:
mcqs.why: A valence (outer) shell holds at most 8 electrons. Atoms try to complete these 8 electrons according to the octet rule.

mcqs.q: Metals gain stability mainly by:
mcqs.why: Metals give electrons from their outer shell to complete the octet of the shell below, forming positive ions. Non-metals take or share electrons.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen follows which rule to become stable?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen is a small atom with one shell, so it follows the duplet rule: it completes 2 electrons in its shell, like helium.

lessons.title: 4.2 Formation of Chemical Bonds
lessons.notes_html:
How Chemical Bonds Form

Atoms form bonds by giving, taking or sharing their valence electrons so that each atom completes its octet or duplet. Metals give electrons and form cations; non-metals gain electrons and form anions, or share electrons.

Ions and Atoms

An ion is a charged atom or group of atoms. An atom is neutral, whereas an ion forms by gaining or losing electrons and is positive (cation) or negative (anion).

Formation of Cations (metals give electrons)

  • K (2, 8, 8, 1) → K+ (2, 8, 8) + e−. A Group IIIA atom gives up 3 electrons; magnesium gives 2 electrons.
  • Al (2, 8, 3) → Al3+ (2, 8) + 3e−.
  • Magnesium's arrangement is 2, 8, 2. It readily gives two electrons because by giving them it becomes Mg2+ and gains a stable octet. Magnesium is in Group IIA and its ion carries a +2 charge, symbol Mg2+.
  • An atom with 2 electrons in its valence shell: magnesium (Mg), arrangement 2, 8, 2.

Formation of Anions (non-metals gain electrons)

  • Oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons to form O2− and completes its octet: O + 2e− → O2− (arrangement 2, 8).
  • S + 2e− → S2− (arrangement 2, 8, 8).
  • N + 3e− → N3−; Br + e− → Br−; P + 3e− → P3−.
  • A non-metal atom gets a negative charge by gaining electrons, e.g. Cl + e− → Cl−.
  • The fluoride ion (F−) has 10 electrons, the same as neon (Ne), so its arrangement is neon-like. By sharing one electron in bonding, a fluorine atom also gets the configuration of neon.

Dot-and-Cross Diagrams

  • H2 (covalent): H• + •H → H:H; both H atoms share electrons.
  • KF (ionic): K (2, 8, 8, 1) gives its one electron to F (2, 7); K+ and F− form and join by attraction.
