mcqs.q: How many electrons does a Group IIIA atom give up?
mcqs.why: A Group IIIA atom has 3 electrons in its outer shell and gives up 3 electrons, e.g. Al (2, 8, 3) → Al3+ (2, 8) + 3e−.

mcqs.q: Which atom gives 2 electrons from its outer shell?
mcqs.why: Magnesium gives 2 electrons; its arrangement is 2, 8, 2 and it forms Mg2+. Potassium gives only 1 electron.

mcqs.q: How does a non-metal atom get a negative charge?
mcqs.why: A non-metal atom gains electrons to get a negative charge, e.g. Cl + e− → Cl− and O + 2e− → O2−.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are in the valence shell of oxygen (Group VIA)?
mcqs.why: Oxygen is in Group VIA and its arrangement is 2, 6, so it has 6 electrons in the valence shell.

mcqs.q: Why is the fluoride ion (F−) considered like neon?
options: It has 10 electrons, the same as neon
mcqs.why: The fluoride ion (F−) has 10 electrons (9 + 1 gained), the same as neon (Ne), so its electron arrangement is neon-like.

mcqs.q: An ion is:
options: A charged atom or group of atoms
mcqs.why: An ion is a charged atom or group of atoms. It differs from an atom because an atom is neutral, while an ion is positive (cation) or negative (anion).

mcqs.q: Why does a magnesium atom readily give two electrons?
options: It wants to become a gas
By giving two electrons it becomes Mg2+ with a stable octet
mcqs.why: Magnesium's arrangement is 2, 8, 2. By giving two electrons it becomes Mg2+ (2, 8) and gains a stable octet.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is in which group, and what is the charge on its ion?
mcqs.why: Magnesium is in Group IIA with 2 electrons in its outer shell (2, 8, 2); its ion carries a +2 charge and its symbol is Mg2+.

mcqs.q: Oxygen forms the oxide ion by:
mcqs.why: Oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons to form O2− and completes its octet: O + 2e− → O2−, giving the arrangement 2, 8.

mcqs.q: In the dot-cross diagram of KF, potassium:
options: Gives its one electron to fluorine, forming K+ and F−
mcqs.why: K (2, 8, 8, 1) gives its one electron to F (2, 7); the ions K+ and F− form and join by attraction — an ionic bond.

lessons.title: 4.3 Types of Chemical Bonds
lessons.notes_html:
Ionic Bond

An ionic bond forms by the transfer of electrons: one atom gives electrons, the other takes them; ions form and join by the attraction of opposite charges. Ionic compounds are compounds formed by the attraction between positive and negative ions, such as NaCl and MgO.

Formation of NaCl: Na (2, 8, 1) gives its one electron to become Na+; Cl (2, 8, 7) takes an electron to become Cl−. The attraction of opposite charges forms NaCl.

Covalent Bond

A covalent bond forms by sharing electron pairs, so that both atoms complete their octets.

  • Single covalent bond: one shared pair, e.g. H2, Cl2.
  • Double covalent bond: two shared pairs.
  • Triple covalent bond: three shared pairs, e.g. N2.
  • Non-polar covalent bond: the electron pair is shared equally, e.g. H2 and Cl2 (atoms of equal electronegativity show no + or − marks).
  • Polar covalent bond: the pair is pulled more towards the more electronegative atom; polarity occurs in molecules such as HCl, H2O and NH3.

Coordinate Covalent Bond

A coordinate covalent bond is a bond in which the shared electron pair is given by only one atom and accepted by the other. Examples: in NH4+, nitrogen gives its lone pair to H+; in H3O+, oxygen gives its lone pair to H+. A coordinate covalent bond is always a polar bond, because the pair comes from one atom only, so partial charges separate in the bond.

Metallic Bond

A metallic bond is the bond between metal atoms in which the valence electrons are shared by all the atoms and form a sea of electrons. Positive metal ions are held in this sea.

Lone Pair and Bond Pair

A lone pair does not take part in bonding and stays on one atom. A bond pair (shared pair) is shared between two atoms and forms a bond — it is the electron pair an atom contributes in bonding.

Bond Nature from Electronegativity Difference

Electronegativity differenceType of bond
0 to 0.4Non-polar covalent
0.4 to 1.7Polar covalent
More than 1.7Ionic bond

When the electronegativity of two atoms differs, the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, so the bond gains partial ionic character. The greater the difference, the greater the ionic character. When opposite partial charges appear on the two sides of a bond, that bond becomes dipolar (polar).

Why Metals Form Ionic but Not Covalent Bonds

Metals like to give electrons, so they form ions and make ionic bonds. A covalent bond requires sharing electrons, which is not the nature of metals.

Dot-Cross Structures of Molecules

  • H2O: O in the centre, single bonds to two H atoms, two lone pairs on O.
  • N2: N≡N triple bond, one lone pair on each N.
  • CH4: C in the centre, single bonds to 4 H atoms.
  • C2H2: H–C≡C–H.
  • Cl2: Cl–Cl single bond. H2: H–H single bond.
  • CCl4: carbon in the centre forming single bonds to 4 chlorines; each chlorine has 3 lone pairs and carbon's octet is complete.
  • A hydrogen atom cannot form more than one covalent bond, because it has only 1 electron and needs only one more electron to complete its duplet.

Polar vs Non-Polar Compounds

  • Polar compounds: partially charged, soluble in water, higher melting and boiling points.
  • Non-polar compounds: uncharged, insoluble in water, lower melting and boiling points.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of an ionic compound?
mcqs.why: NaCl is an ionic compound because it forms by the transfer of electrons from sodium to chlorine. H2, CH4 and N2 are covalent.

mcqs.q: When one atom donates an electron pair and the other accepts it, which bond is formed?
mcqs.why: A coordinate covalent bond forms when the shared electron pair is given by only one atom, e.g. the N atom gives its lone pair to H+ in NH4+.

mcqs.q: What is a bond called in which three electron pairs are shared?
mcqs.why: A bond with three shared electron pairs is a triple covalent bond, such as the N≡N bond in N2.

mcqs.q: When two atoms share an electron pair equally, the bond is called:
mcqs.why: Equal sharing of an electron pair gives a non-polar covalent bond, such as in H2 and Cl2, where both atoms have equal electronegativity.

mcqs.q: Which bond forms by sharing electrons?
mcqs.why: A covalent bond forms by sharing electron pairs between atoms, so that both atoms complete their octets.

mcqs.q: Which electron pair does an atom contribute in bonding?
mcqs.why: The pair an atom contributes in bonding is the shared pair, which is also called the bond pair. A lone pair stays on one atom and does not form a bond.

mcqs.q: The difference between a lone pair and a bond pair is:
options: A lone pair stays on one atom and does not bond; a bond pair is shared between two atoms
mcqs.why: A lone pair does not take part in bonding and stays on one atom, while a bond pair is shared between two atoms and forms the bond.

mcqs.q: If the electronegativity difference between two atoms is more than 1.7, the bond is:
mcqs.why: Difference 0 to 0.4 gives non-polar covalent, 0.4 to 1.7 gives polar covalent, and more than 1.7 gives an ionic bond.

mcqs.q: Ionic compounds are:
options: Compounds formed by the attraction between positive and negative ions, such as NaCl and MgO
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds are formed by the attraction between positive and negative ions, such as NaCl and MgO, after the transfer of electrons.

mcqs.q: In the formation of NaCl:
options: Na and Cl share two pairs
Na gives its one electron to Cl, forming Na+ and Cl− which attract each other
Cl gives an electron to Na
mcqs.why: Na (2, 8, 1) gives its one electron to become Na+, and Cl (2, 8, 7) takes it to become Cl−. The attraction of opposite charges forms NaCl — an ionic bond.

mcqs.q: A metallic bond is:
options: Transfer of electrons to a non-metal
A sea of shared valence electrons holding positive metal ions
mcqs.why: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons are shared by all the metal atoms and form a sea of electrons in which the positive metal ions are held.

mcqs.q: A coordinate covalent bond is always a polar bond because:
options: The shared pair is given by one atom only, so partial charges separate
mcqs.why: In a coordinate covalent bond the shared electron pair comes from only one atom, so partial charges separate in the bond and the bond has polar character.

mcqs.q: Why can a hydrogen atom not form more than one covalent bond?
options: It has only 1 electron and needs only one more to complete its duplet
It is too small to hold bonds
mcqs.why: Hydrogen has only 1 electron and needs only one more electron to complete its duplet, so it forms only one covalent bond.

mcqs.q: Polarity occurs in a molecule in which:
options: Atoms differ in electronegativity, such as HCl, H2O and NH3
mcqs.why: Polarity occurs when the atoms of a molecule differ in electronegativity, e.g. HCl, H2O and NH3, so the shared pair is pulled to one side.

mcqs.q: In CCl4, the dot-cross structure shows carbon:
options: With a triple bond to chlorine
In the centre with single bonds to 4 chlorines, each chlorine having 3 lone pairs
mcqs.why: In CCl4, carbon is in the centre and forms single bonds to 4 chlorine atoms; each chlorine has 3 lone pairs and carbon's octet is complete.

lessons.title: 4.4 Intermolecular Forces
lessons.notes_html:
What are Intermolecular Forces?

The intermolecular force is the weak attraction that holds neighbouring molecules together. It is weaker than the intramolecular force because intramolecular forces are strong chemical bonds between atoms, whereas intermolecular forces are only weak attractions between molecules.

Hydrogen Bond

The mutual interaction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom is called a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonding holds molecules close together, so:

  • Melting and boiling points rise.
  • Solubility in water increases.
  • Special properties, such as those of water, appear.

Dipole-Dipole Force

The dipole force is the attraction between polar molecules: the positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another molecule.

mcqs.q: The mutual interaction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom is called:
mcqs.why: This attraction is called a hydrogen bond. It acts between molecules in substances like water and raises their boiling points.

mcqs.q: The intermolecular force is:
options: A strong chemical bond inside a molecule
The weak attraction that holds neighbouring molecules together
mcqs.why: The intermolecular force is the weak attraction between neighbouring molecules, e.g. hydrogen bonds and dipole forces.

mcqs.q: Why is the intermolecular force weaker than the intramolecular force?
options: Intramolecular forces are strong chemical bonds between atoms, while intermolecular forces are weak attractions between molecules
mcqs.why: Intramolecular forces are strong chemical bonds between atoms, whereas intermolecular forces are weak attractions between molecules, so they are weaker.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen bonding affects the physical properties of compounds by:
options: Holding molecules close, so melting and boiling points rise and solubility in water increases
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding holds molecules close together, so melting and boiling points rise, solubility in water increases, and special properties such as those of water appear.

mcqs.q: The dipole-dipole force is:
options: Attraction between polar molecules — the positive end of one attracts the negative end of another
mcqs.why: The dipole-dipole force is the attraction between polar molecules: the positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another.

mcqs.q: Water has special properties (high boiling point for its size) mainly due to:
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding holds water molecules close together, which raises its melting and boiling points and gives water its special properties.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an intermolecular force?
mcqs.why: A hydrogen bond between water molecules acts between molecules, so it is an intermolecular force. The others act inside a substance's particles.

mcqs.q: On melting a covalent substance, what breaks first?
options: The strong covalent bonds inside molecules
The weak intermolecular forces between molecules
mcqs.why: On melting, the weak forces between molecules break, not the strong inner bonds, which is why most covalent substances have low melting points.

mcqs.q: Polar molecules attract each other through:
mcqs.why: Polar molecules attract each other through dipole-dipole forces: the positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another.

mcqs.q: Intermolecular forces are present:
options: Between neighbouring molecules in a substance
mcqs.why: Intermolecular forces are the weak attractions that hold neighbouring molecules together in solids, liquids and (weakly) in gases.

lessons.title: 4.5 Nature and Properties of Bonds
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Ionic Compounds

  • They are crystalline solids at room temperature.
  • They have high melting and boiling points, because the attraction between ions is very strong.
  • They conduct electricity in the molten or dissolved state, but not as solids.
  • They are hard and brittle.
  • In the NaCl crystal, each Na+ ion is surrounded by 6 Cl− ions.

Why Covalent Compounds Have Low Melting Points

The covalent bonds inside a molecule are strong, but the forces between molecules are weak. On melting, the weak forces between molecules break, not the inner bonds, so the melting point is low — e.g. ice. Compared with an ionic bond, a covalent bond's effect is weaker in this sense: the ionic bond is stronger because of the strong attraction between ions.

Properties of Metallic Bonds

In a metallic bond, metal atoms are joined in a sea of electrons. That is why metals are:

  • Good conductors of heat and electricity — metals have free/shared electrons which move easily and carry heat and electricity from one place to another.
  • Shiny (lustrous).
  • Malleable (can be beaten into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires).

Adhesives and Epoxy Adhesives

Adhesives are used to join broken things, to stick wood, paper, cloth and plastic, and to join parts in electronics — where electrical insulation/barrier is needed. Epoxy adhesives are very strong and are used in electronics, aircraft and buildings. Adhesives are important in society for daily repairs and for joining parts in industry.

mcqs.q: In the NaCl crystal structure, each Na+ is surrounded by how many Cl− ions?
mcqs.why: In the NaCl crystal, each Na+ ion is surrounded by 6 Cl− ions, and each Cl− by 6 Na+ ions, in a regular crystal lattice.

mcqs.q: In what state are ionic compounds mostly found at room temperature?
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds are mostly crystalline solids at room temperature because of the strong attraction between their ions in the lattice.

mcqs.q: Ionic crystals have:
mcqs.why: Ionic crystals have high melting points because the attraction between the positive and negative ions is very strong and needs much heat to break.

mcqs.q: Compared with an ionic bond, the covalent bond's strength in holding a solid together is:
options: Weak — the ionic bond is stronger
mcqs.why: The ionic bond is stronger because of the strong attraction between ions throughout the crystal; covalent solids are held by weak forces between molecules.

mcqs.q: Why is the melting point of a covalent compound like ice low?
options: Between covalent molecules there are weak intermolecular forces, which break with little heat
mcqs.why: Between covalent molecules there are weak intermolecular forces, which break with little heat, so the melting point is low, although the bonds inside the molecules are strong.

mcqs.q: Covalent bonds are strong, yet most covalent molecules have low melting points, because:
options: On melting, the weak forces between molecules break, not the inner bonds
mcqs.why: The bonds inside a molecule are strong, but the forces between molecules are weak. On melting only the weak between-molecule forces break, so the melting point is low.

mcqs.q: Which is a property of ionic compounds?
options: They are hard and brittle crystalline solids
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds are crystalline solids, hard and brittle, with high melting and boiling points; they conduct electricity only in the molten or dissolved state.

mcqs.q: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity because:
options: They have free/shared electrons which move easily and carry heat and electricity
mcqs.why: Metals have free electrons in the sea of electrons, which move easily and carry heat and electricity from one place to another.

mcqs.q: In a metallic bond, the sea of electrons makes metals:
mcqs.why: Because metal atoms are joined in a sea of electrons, metals are good conductors, shiny, malleable (beaten into sheets) and ductile (drawn into wires).

mcqs.q: Epoxy adhesives are used in electronics because there they provide:
mcqs.why: Adhesives are used where an electrical insulation/barrier is needed, and epoxy adhesives are very strong; they are used in electronics, aircraft and buildings for joining parts.

lessons.title: 5.1 Gaseous State
lessons.notes_html:
The Gaseous State

In a gas, the particles are very far apart and move freely in all directions, so a gas has no fixed shape or volume and its density is low — gas is the lightest form of matter among solid, liquid and gas.

Kinetic Molecular Theory and the States of Matter

  • In a solid, the particles are close and only vibrate in place.
  • In a liquid, the particles can flow over one another.
  • In a gas, the particles are far apart and move freely.
  • As temperature rises, the motion of the particles increases.

Diffusion and Effusion

  • Diffusion: the spontaneous spreading of gas or liquid molecules due to random motion, such as perfume spreading in a room. Lighter gases spread faster.
  • Effusion: gas escaping through a tiny hole, such as gas leaking from a balloon.
  • Both depend on molar mass (Graham's law), temperature and pressure. Hydrogen diffuses fastest because it is the lightest gas (molecular mass = 2).

Effect of Heat on a Gas

On heating, a gas expands and its volume increases, so its density decreases.

mcqs.q: Which gas diffuses fastest?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen diffuses fastest because it is the lightest gas (molecular mass = 2). By Graham's law, lighter gases spread faster.

mcqs.q: Which is the lightest matter among the following?
mcqs.why: Gas is the lightest because its particles are very far apart and its density is low compared with liquids and solids.

mcqs.q: Diffusion is:
options: Gas escaping through a tiny hole
The spontaneous spreading of molecules due to random motion
mcqs.why: Diffusion is the spontaneous spreading of gas or liquid molecules, such as perfume spreading in a room. Effusion is escape through a tiny hole.

mcqs.q: Effusion is:
options: Spreading of perfume in a room
Gas escaping through a tiny hole, such as from a balloon
mcqs.why: Effusion is the escape of a gas through a tiny hole, such as gas leaking from a balloon. Diffusion is the general spreading of molecules.

mcqs.q: According to kinetic molecular theory, in a gas the particles:
options: Are far apart and move freely
mcqs.why: In a gas the particles are far apart and move freely. In a solid they only vibrate in place, and in a liquid they flow over one another.

mcqs.q: When a gas is heated, its density:
options: Decreases, because it expands and its volume increases
mcqs.why: On heating, the gas expands and its volume increases, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and the density decreases.

mcqs.q: Diffusion and effusion depend on:
mcqs.why: Both diffusion and effusion depend on molar mass (Graham's law), temperature and pressure. Lighter gases diffuse and effuse faster.

mcqs.q: Perfume spreading in a room is an example of:
mcqs.why: Perfume spreading in a room is diffusion — the spontaneous spreading of gas molecules due to their random motion.

mcqs.q: As temperature rises, the motion of the particles of matter:
mcqs.why: According to kinetic molecular theory, as temperature rises the motion (kinetic energy) of the particles increases in every state of matter.

mcqs.q: In a solid, according to kinetic theory, the particles:
options: Are close together and only vibrate in place
mcqs.why: In a solid the particles are close and only vibrate in place, which is why solids have fixed shape and volume.

lessons.title: 5.2 Gas Laws
lessons.notes_html:
Pressure and Temperature Units

  • One atmosphere pressure = 101325 pascal (Pa).
  • Temperature conversion: K = °C + 273; °C = K − 273.
  • Absolute zero is −273°C (0 K), the temperature at which the volume of a gas would become zero and molecular motion almost stops.

Conversions — Worked Examples

  • 100°C = 100 + 273 = 373 K
  • 150°C = 150 + 273 = 423 K
  • 750 K = 750 − 273 = 477°C
  • 170 K = 170 − 273 = −103°C

Boyle's Law

At constant temperature, the volume of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

Formula: PV = K, i.e. P1V1 = P2V2. In Boyle's law, pressure (P) and volume (V) are the variables, while temperature stays constant.

Example: pressing air in a syringe decreases its volume and increases its pressure.

Example 1: A gas at STP occupies 40.0 dm³; at constant temperature the pressure becomes 3 atm. New volume?

P1V1 = P2V2 → V2 = 1 × 40.0 ÷ 3 = 13.33 dm³

Example 2: A gas of 800 cm³ at 750 mm Hg is compressed to 250 cm³. New pressure?

P1V1 = P2V2 → P2 = 800 × 750 ÷ 250 = 2400 mm Hg

Example 3: A gas sample at 8 atm has volume 15 litres; pressure is brought to 6 atm. New volume?

P1V1 = P2V2 → V2 = 8 × 15 ÷ 6 = 20 litres

Charles's Law

At constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. When temperature increases, a gas expands (at constant pressure).

Formula: V/T = K, i.e. V1/T1 = V2/T2. On a graph, the relation between volume and temperature is a straight line.

Example: warming a balloon makes it expand.

Example 1: A gas expands from 90.5 cm³ to 120 cm³ at constant pressure; initial temperature is 33°C. Final temperature?

T1 = 33 + 273 = 306 K

T2 = V2 × T1 ÷ V1 = 120 × 306 ÷ 90.5 = 405.6 K = 132.6°C

Example 2: A gas of 78 ml at constant pressure is heated from 35°C to 80°C. Final volume?

T1 = 35 + 273 = 308 K; T2 = 80 + 273 = 353 K

V2 = V1 × T2 ÷ T1 = 78 × 353 ÷ 308 = 89.4 ml

mcqs.why: One atmosphere pressure equals 101325 pascal. It is the standard atmospheric pressure at sea level.

mcqs.why: A gas expands when its temperature increases at constant pressure, according to Charles's law: volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

options: Pressure and volume, while temperature stays constant
mcqs.why: In Boyle's law, pressure (P) and volume (V) are the variables, while the temperature stays constant.

mcqs.q: Charles's law states that at constant pressure:
mcqs.why: Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, i.e. V/T = K.

A gas at STP occupies 40.0 dm³. At constant temperature its pressure becomes 3 atm. The new volume is:
mcqs.why: By Boyle's law P1V1 = P2V2, so V2 = 1 × 40.0 ÷ 3 = 13.33 dm³. Increasing the pressure three times decreases the volume to one-third.

mcqs.why: P1V1 = P2V2, so P2 = 800 × 750 ÷ 250 = 2400 mm Hg. Compressing the gas raises its pressure.

options: −273°C (0 K), where the volume of a gas would become zero and molecular motion almost stops
mcqs.why: Absolute zero is −273°C (0 K), the lowest possible temperature, at which the volume of a gas would become zero and molecular motion almost stops.
