lessons.title: 5.3 Liquid State
lessons.notes_html:
The Liquid State

In a liquid, the particles are close but can flow over one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape.

Evaporation

Evaporation is the process in which liquid molecules escape from the surface as vapour at any temperature. The molecules that leave are those which have more energy, so they escape the intermolecular attraction and leave the surface.

  • Factors affecting evaporation: temperature, surface area, air movement, intermolecular forces and the nature of the liquid. External pressure does not affect the rate of evaporation much, because evaporation happens at the surface.
  • Evaporation increases with temperature: as temperature rises, more molecules gain enough energy to escape from the surface as vapour.
  • Evaporation causes cooling because the higher-energy molecules leave and the average energy of the remaining molecules falls.

Vapour Pressure

Vapour pressure is the pressure of a liquid's vapour above the liquid. It occurs in a closed system: the vapour cannot escape, so equilibrium is set up between evaporation and condensation and the pressure becomes constant — this is called dynamic equilibrium, in which the rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation. The vapour pressure of water increases with temperature, because as temperature rises more molecules become vapour.

Boiling Point

  • Boiling point: the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals atmospheric pressure and the liquid starts to boil.
  • The boiling point depends on pressure: when atmospheric pressure rises, the boiling point rises; when it falls, the boiling point falls — for example, on mountains water boils below 100°C.
  • Freezing point: the temperature at which a liquid becomes a solid. Melting point: the temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid.

Diffusion in Liquids

Diffusion in liquids is the spreading of the molecules of one liquid through another, such as ink spreading in water. It is affected by temperature, particle size and the density of the liquid. The rate of diffusion in liquids is lower than in gases because in a liquid the molecules are close and held by strong attraction, so they move slowly — ink spreads slowly in water, while perfume spreads quickly in air.

mcqs.q: The vapour pressure of water increases with:
mcqs.why: The vapour pressure of water increases with temperature, because as temperature rises, more molecules gain energy and become vapour.

mcqs.q: On what does the boiling point depend?
options: Pressure — it rises when atmospheric pressure rises
mcqs.why: The boiling point depends on pressure: when atmospheric pressure rises the boiling point rises, and on mountains, where pressure is low, water boils below 100°C.

mcqs.q: Which of the following does NOT affect the rate of evaporation?
mcqs.why: External pressure does not affect the rate of evaporation much, because evaporation happens at the surface in open space. Temperature, surface area and the nature of the liquid do affect it.

mcqs.q: In evaporation, molecules leave the liquid surface because they have:
options: More energy, so they escape the intermolecular attraction
mcqs.why: Only the molecules with more energy can escape the intermolecular attraction and leave the surface as vapour; this is evaporation.

mcqs.q: Evaporation causes cooling because:
options: The higher-energy molecules leave and the average energy of the remaining molecules falls
mcqs.why: The molecules that evaporate carry away more energy, so the average energy of the molecules left behind falls and the liquid cools.

mcqs.q: Vapour pressure is set up in a closed system because:
options: The vapour cannot escape, so evaporation and condensation reach a dynamic equilibrium
mcqs.why: In a closed system the vapour cannot escape, so the rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation and the vapour pressure becomes constant (dynamic equilibrium).

mcqs.q: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which:
options: Its vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure and it starts to boil
mcqs.why: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the atmospheric pressure. Below this temperature only evaporation from the surface takes place.

mcqs.q: Why does a rise in temperature increase evaporation?
options: More molecules gain enough energy to escape from the surface as vapour
mcqs.why: As temperature rises, more molecules gain enough energy to overcome the intermolecular attraction and escape from the surface as vapour.

mcqs.q: The rate of diffusion in liquids is lower than in gases because:
options: Liquid molecules are close and held by strong attraction, so they move slowly
mcqs.why: In a liquid the molecules are close and held by strong attraction, so they move slowly; ink spreads slowly in water, while perfume spreads quickly in air.

mcqs.q: On mountains, water boils below 100°C because:
options: Atmospheric pressure is lower, so the boiling point falls
mcqs.why: When atmospheric pressure falls, the boiling point falls. On mountains the pressure is low, so water boils below 100°C.

lessons.title: 5.4 Solid State
lessons.notes_html:
The Solid State

In a solid, the particles are packed close together and only vibrate in place — that is why the particles of a solid are the slowest-moving, and a solid has a definite shape and volume.

Effect of Melting Points on Solids

  • Solids with higher melting points have stronger bonds and melt slowly on heating, such as diamond.
  • Solids with lower melting points melt quickly, such as ice and wax.

So the melting point of a solid shows the strength of the forces holding its particles: strong forces need more heat to break, and weak forces break with little heat.

mcqs.q: In which state are the slowest-moving particles?
mcqs.why: The particles of a solid are the slowest-moving because in a solid the particles only vibrate in place and cannot move freely.

mcqs.q: In a solid, the particles:
options: Are packed close and only vibrate in place
mcqs.why: In a solid the particles are close together and only vibrate in place, which gives a solid its definite shape and volume.

mcqs.q: A solid has a definite shape and volume because:
options: Its particles are held close in fixed positions
mcqs.why: The particles of a solid are packed close in fixed positions and only vibrate, so the solid keeps a definite shape and volume.

mcqs.q: Solids with higher melting points melt slowly on heating because they have:
mcqs.why: Solids with higher melting points have stronger bonds between their particles, so more heat is needed and they melt slowly, such as diamond.

mcqs.q: Which solid melts quickly because of its low melting point?
mcqs.why: Ice (and wax) have low melting points and melt quickly, while diamond has a very high melting point because of its strong bonds.

mcqs.q: Diamond melts slowly on heating because:
options: It has very strong bonds and a high melting point
mcqs.why: Diamond has stronger bonds and a higher melting point, so it melts slowly on heating; solids with lower melting points, like ice and wax, melt quickly.

mcqs.q: The melting point of a solid indicates:
options: The strength of the forces holding its particles
mcqs.why: A high melting point means strong forces between particles; a low melting point means weak forces that break with little heat.

mcqs.q: Compared with gases, the particles of a solid are:
mcqs.why: Solid particles are packed very close together, unlike gas particles which are far apart and move freely.

mcqs.q: When a solid is heated strongly, its particles:
options: Vibrate more and may break free at the melting point
mcqs.why: Heating makes the particles vibrate more; at the melting point the particles of a weak-bonded solid like ice break free quickly, while diamond needs much more heat.

mcqs.q: Wax melts quickly on gentle heating because:
options: It has a low melting point and weak forces
mcqs.why: Wax has a lower melting point, so it melts quickly; solids with higher melting points have stronger bonds and melt slowly.

lessons.title: 5.5 Types of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Solids

Crystalline solidsAmorphous solids
Particles arranged in a regular, orderly patternParticles arranged in disorder
Have a definite (sharp) melting pointHave no definite melting point; soften gradually
Examples: diamond, saltExamples: glass, plastic, rubber

Diamond is a crystalline solid, so it has a definite melting point. Glass, plastic and rubber are amorphous solids and do not melt at one sharp temperature.

mcqs.q: Which solid has a definite melting point?
mcqs.why: Diamond has a definite melting point because it is a crystalline solid with particles in a regular order. Glass, plastic and rubber are amorphous.

mcqs.q: Crystalline solids differ from amorphous solids because crystalline solids:
options: Have particles in a regular order and a definite melting point
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have particles in order and a definite melting point, e.g. diamond and salt. Amorphous solids have disordered particles and no definite melting point.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an amorphous solid?
mcqs.why: Glass is an amorphous solid — its particles are in disorder and it has no definite melting point. Diamond and salt are crystalline.

mcqs.q: Amorphous solids have:
options: No definite melting point and soften gradually
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids such as glass, plastic and rubber have disordered particles and no definite melting point; they soften over a range of temperature.

mcqs.q: Common salt (NaCl) is an example of:
mcqs.why: Salt is a crystalline solid with a regular arrangement of particles and a definite melting point.

mcqs.q: Plastic and rubber are examples of:
mcqs.why: Plastic and rubber are amorphous solids: their particles are in disorder and they have no definite melting point.

mcqs.q: A solid whose particles are arranged in a regular pattern is called:
mcqs.why: A crystalline solid has its particles arranged in a regular, orderly pattern, e.g. diamond and salt, and it melts at a definite temperature.

mcqs.q: Diamond has a definite melting point because it is:
mcqs.why: Diamond is a crystalline solid with an orderly arrangement of carbon atoms, so it has a definite melting point, unlike glass or plastic.

mcqs.q: Which pair contains only amorphous solids?
mcqs.why: Glass and plastic are both amorphous solids with disordered particles. Diamond, salt and ice are crystalline.

mcqs.q: Amorphous solids soften gradually on heating because:
options: They have a sharp melting point
Their particles are in disorder, so different parts soften at different temperatures
mcqs.why: Because the particles of an amorphous solid are in disorder, there is no single melting temperature; the solid softens gradually, as glass and plastic do.

lessons.title: 5.6 Allotropy
lessons.notes_html:
What is Allotropy?

Allotropy is the property in which the same element occurs in different forms. These different forms of an element are called allotropes. They have the same chemical element but different arrangements of atoms, so their physical properties differ.

Allotropes of Carbon

  • Diamond: a hard crystalline form of carbon with a definite melting point.
  • Graphite: another crystalline form of carbon, different in structure from diamond.
  • Fullerenes: a third form of carbon with cage-like molecules.

mcqs.q: Allotropy is the property in which:
options: The same element occurs in different forms
mcqs.why: Allotropy is the property in which the same element occurs in different forms, e.g. carbon occurs as diamond, graphite and fullerenes.

mcqs.q: Diamond, graphite and fullerenes are allotropes of:
mcqs.why: Diamond, graphite and fullerenes are the allotropes of carbon — the same element, carbon, in three different forms.

mcqs.q: The different forms of an element in allotropy are called:
mcqs.why: The different forms of the same element are called allotropes. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

mcqs.q: Allotropes of an element differ in:
options: The arrangement of atoms and physical properties
mcqs.why: Allotropes contain the same kind of atoms but in different arrangements, so their physical properties — like hardness and structure — differ.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an allotrope of carbon?
mcqs.why: Fullerenes are an allotrope of carbon, along with diamond and graphite. Carbon dioxide and methane are compounds of carbon, not its forms.

mcqs.q: Diamond and graphite are both made of:
mcqs.why: Both diamond and graphite are pure carbon; they are allotropes because their carbon atoms are arranged in different structures.

mcqs.q: Allotropy is shown by the element:
mcqs.why: Carbon shows allotropy — it occurs as diamond, graphite and fullerenes, the same element in different forms.

mcqs.q: The hardness difference between diamond and graphite is due to:
options: Different arrangement of the same carbon atoms
mcqs.why: Diamond and graphite are both carbon; their very different hardness comes from the different arrangement of atoms in the two allotropes.

mcqs.q: Fullerenes are:
options: A form (allotrope) of carbon with cage-like molecules
mcqs.why: Fullerenes are an allotrope of carbon — a different form of the same element, with cage-like arrangements of carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Which statement about allotropes is correct?
options: They have different numbers of protons
They are the same element in different forms
mcqs.why: Allotropes are the same element occurring in different forms, e.g. diamond, graphite and fullerenes are all carbon.

lessons.title: 5.7 Plasma State
lessons.notes_html:
What is Plasma?

Plasma is the fourth state of matter. In plasma, the gas atoms split into ions and free electrons because of very high temperature or energy. It is a mixture of positive ions and free electrons.

Examples of Plasma in Daily Life

  • Lightning in the sky.
  • Neon lights and sign tubes.
  • TV screens (plasma screens).
  • Plasma lamps.

mcqs.q: Plasma is which state of matter?
mcqs.why: Plasma is the fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid and gas. In it, gas atoms split into ions and free electrons.

mcqs.q: In plasma, the gas atoms split into:
mcqs.why: In plasma the gas atoms split into ions and free electrons because of the very high energy, so plasma contains charged particles.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of plasma?
mcqs.why: Lightning is a natural example of plasma. Neon lights, TV screens and plasma lamps are man-made examples.

mcqs.q: Neon lights contain matter in which state?
mcqs.why: The glowing gas inside neon lights is in the plasma state, where the gas atoms have split into ions and free electrons.

mcqs.q: Plasma forms when a gas is:
options: Given very high energy so its atoms ionise
mcqs.why: Plasma forms when a gas receives very high energy (very high temperature), so its atoms split into ions and free electrons.

mcqs.q: Plasma TV screens work with:
options: Plasma — ionised gas in tiny cells
mcqs.why: Plasma TV screens contain ionised gas (plasma) in tiny cells, which glows to form the picture. Plasma lamps work the same way.

mcqs.q: Which particles are present in plasma?
mcqs.why: Plasma is a mixture of positive ions and free electrons formed when gas atoms split apart at very high energy.

mcqs.q: Plasma differs from an ordinary gas because in plasma:
options: Atoms have split into ions and free electrons
mcqs.why: In an ordinary gas the particles are neutral atoms or molecules; in plasma the atoms split into ions and free electrons.

mcqs.q: Which of these contains plasma?
mcqs.why: A plasma lamp contains ionised gas, i.e. plasma. Lightning, neon lights and TV screens are other examples.

mcqs.q: The fourth state of matter is:
mcqs.why: Plasma is called the fourth state of matter. It is found in lightning and is used in neon lights, TV screens and plasma lamps.

lessons.title: 5.8 Bose-Einstein Condensate
lessons.notes_html:
What is Bose-Einstein Condensate?

Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) is a state of matter that forms near absolute zero (0 K, −273°C). It was presented as an idea by S.N. Bose and Albert Einstein, and was first prepared by Eric Cornell, with Carl Wieman making its arrangement.

Why is it Super-Cold and Super-Unexcited?

  • It forms near absolute zero, 0 K = −273°C, so it is super-cold.
  • At such cold, the motion of the atoms almost stops, so it is super-unexcited matter — the atoms have almost no energy of motion.
  • It is the opposite extreme of plasma: plasma forms at very high energy, while BEC forms at almost zero energy.

mcqs.q: Bose-Einstein Condensate forms near which temperature?
mcqs.why: Bose-Einstein Condensate forms near absolute zero (0 K, −273°C), where the motion of atoms almost stops.

mcqs.q: Bose-Einstein Condensate is called super-cold because:
options: It forms near absolute zero where atoms almost stop moving
It is kept in a fridge
mcqs.why: It forms near absolute zero (0 K, −273°C); at such cold the motion of atoms almost stops, so it is super-cold and super-unexcited matter.

mcqs.q: At absolute zero, the motion of atoms:
mcqs.why: At absolute zero (0 K) the motion of atoms almost stops, which is why Bose-Einstein Condensate is called super-unexcited matter.

mcqs.q: The idea of Bose-Einstein Condensate was presented by:
mcqs.why: The state was presented by S.N. Bose and Albert Einstein; it was named after them as the Bose-Einstein Condensate.

mcqs.q: Who first prepared Bose-Einstein Condensate?
mcqs.why: Eric Cornell first prepared Bose-Einstein Condensate, and Carl Wieman made its arrangement (set-up).

mcqs.q: 0 K is equal to:
mcqs.why: 0 K = −273°C. This is absolute zero, the temperature near which Bose-Einstein Condensate forms.

mcqs.q: Bose-Einstein Condensate is called super-unexcited because:
options: Its atoms have almost no motion or energy at near 0 K
mcqs.why: At near absolute zero the atoms almost stop moving, so the matter is super-unexcited — the opposite of the highly excited plasma state.

mcqs.q: Which state of matter forms at almost zero energy?
mcqs.why: Bose-Einstein Condensate forms at almost zero energy (near 0 K), while plasma forms at very high energy.

mcqs.q: Carl Wieman's work on Bose-Einstein Condensate was to:
options: Make the arrangement (set-up) of Bose-Einstein Condensate
mcqs.why: Carl Wieman made the arrangement of Bose-Einstein Condensate, which Eric Cornell first prepared in the laboratory.

mcqs.q: Compared with plasma, Bose-Einstein Condensate forms at:
options: Extremely low temperature near absolute zero
mcqs.why: Plasma forms at very high energy, while Bose-Einstein Condensate forms near absolute zero (0 K, −273°C), where atomic motion almost stops.

lessons.title: 6.1 Solutions, Aqueous Solutions, Solute and Solvent
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Solution?

A solution is a homogeneous mixture formed when a solute dissolves in a solvent. A solution is called a mixture because two or more substances are uniformly mixed in it, without a chemical reaction.

Components of a Solution

  • Solute: the component present in the smaller amount, which dissolves, e.g. salt in salt solution.
  • Solvent: the component present in the larger amount, which dissolves the solute, e.g. water in salt solution.
  • An aqueous solution is a solution in which the solvent is water.
  • In air, nitrogen is the solvent because it is present in the largest amount (about 78%); oxygen and carbon dioxide are solutes.

Properties of a Solution

  • It is a homogeneous mixture.
  • Its particles are very small (smaller than 1 nm).
  • Its particles do not settle down.
  • Light passes through it without scattering.

How Salt Dissolves in Water

When salt is added to water, the polar water molecules attract the Na+ and Cl− ions. The oxygen ends of water surround Na+ and the hydrogen ends surround Cl−, so the salt crystals break apart and dissolve. This process is called hydration. The oxygen end of water is partially negative and the hydrogen end is partially positive.

Importance of Solutions in Life

Most processes in our body and daily life happen in solution, such as food digestion, medicines working and cleaning. For a chemist, solutions are useful because in solutions chemical reactions happen quickly, solutions can be measured, standard solutions can be made, and experiments such as titration can be performed.

mcqs.q: When a solute dissolves in a solvent, the mixture is called:
mcqs.why: When a solute dissolves in a solvent, the homogeneous mixture formed is called a solution, e.g. salt dissolved in water.

mcqs.q: An aqueous solution is a solution in which the solvent is:
mcqs.why: An aqueous solution is a solution in which the solvent is water, e.g. salt solution and sugar solution in water.

mcqs.q: In salt solution, the solute and solvent are:
mcqs.why: Salt is the solute (smaller amount, which dissolves) and water is the solvent (larger amount, which dissolves the salt).

mcqs.q: Air is a gas-in-gas solution. The solvent in air is:
options: Nitrogen, because it is present in the largest amount (about 78%)
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is the solvent in air because it is present in the largest amount (about 78%); oxygen, carbon dioxide and other gases are the solutes.

mcqs.q: A solution is called a mixture because:
options: Two or more substances are uniformly mixed in it without a chemical reaction
mcqs.why: A solution is a mixture because two or more substances are uniformly mixed in it without any chemical reaction taking place.

mcqs.q: Which is a property of a true solution?
options: It is homogeneous and its particles do not settle
mcqs.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with very small particles (smaller than 1 nm) which do not settle, and light passes through it.

mcqs.q: The process in which water molecules surround the ions of salt and dissolve it is called:
mcqs.why: Hydration: the oxygen ends of water surround Na+ and the hydrogen ends surround Cl−, so the salt crystal breaks apart and dissolves.

mcqs.q: The oxygen end of a water molecule is:
options: Partially negative, so it attracts Na+
mcqs.why: The oxygen end of water is partially negative and attracts Na+, while the partially positive hydrogen ends attract Cl−; this is hydration.

mcqs.q: Why are solutions important in our life?
options: Most body and daily-life processes happen in solution, such as digestion and medicines working
mcqs.why: Most processes in our body and daily life happen in solution, such as food digestion, medicines working and cleaning.

mcqs.q: For a chemist, solutions are useful because:
options: Reactions happen quickly in solutions and standard solutions can be made for titration
mcqs.why: In solutions, chemical reactions happen quickly, solutions can be measured, standard solutions can be made, and experiments such as titration can be performed.

lessons.title: 6.2 Saturated, Unsaturated and Supersaturated Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
Saturated Solution

A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute at that temperature; extra solute added to it stays undissolved.

Unsaturated Solution

An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute. It is prepared by dissolving less solute than the solubility limit. Heating a saturated KCl solution makes it unsaturated, because on heating more solute can dissolve.

Supersaturated Solution

When a saturated solution is cooled, it can become supersaturated: cooling lowers the solubility and the extra solute stays dissolved in the solution. A supersaturated solution is prepared by heating a saturated solution to dissolve more solute, then cooling it slowly without disturbance.

Beaker Experiment

Beaker A (20 mL water + 10 g sodium thiosulphate, all dissolved) has the unsaturated solution, while beaker B, with more solute (20 g) and undissolved solid remaining, has the saturated solution.

mcqs.q: Heating a saturated KCl solution makes it:
mcqs.why: Heating a saturated solution makes it unsaturated, because on heating the solubility increases and more solute can dissolve.

mcqs.q: When a saturated solution is cooled, it becomes:
mcqs.why: On cooling, a saturated solution becomes supersaturated because cooling lowers the solubility and the extra solute stays dissolved in the solution.

mcqs.q: A saturated solution is one in which:
options: The maximum solute is dissolved at that temperature and extra solute stays undissolved
mcqs.why: A saturated solution holds the maximum solute at that temperature; any extra solute remains undissolved at the bottom.

mcqs.q: An unsaturated solution is prepared by:
options: Dissolving more than the solubility limit
Dissolving less solute than the solubility limit
mcqs.why: An unsaturated solution still can dissolve more solute; it is prepared by dissolving less solute than the solubility limit.

mcqs.q: A supersaturated solution is prepared by:
options: Heating a saturated solution to dissolve more solute, then cooling it slowly without disturbance
mcqs.why: The saturated solution is heated to dissolve more solute, then cooled slowly without disturbance, so more solute stays dissolved than at saturation — a supersaturated solution.

mcqs.q: Beaker A has 20 mL water + 10 g sodium thiosulphate (all dissolved); beaker B has 20 g with solid remaining. Beaker A is:
mcqs.why: Beaker A has the unsaturated solution because it has less solute and all of it dissolves; beaker B, with undissolved solid remaining, is saturated.

mcqs.q: Which beaker in the above experiment has the saturated solution?
options: Beaker B, because it has more solute and undissolved solid remains
mcqs.why: Beaker B has the saturated solution because it has more solute and the undissolved solid remains, showing no more can dissolve.

mcqs.q: If a saturated solution is heated, it can dissolve more solute because:
options: Solubility of most solids increases with temperature
mcqs.why: The solubility of most solid solutes increases with temperature, so a heated saturated solution becomes unsaturated and can dissolve more solute.

mcqs.q: A solution that can still dissolve more solute at that temperature is called:
mcqs.why: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute. A saturated solution cannot, and a supersaturated solution holds extra solute after slow cooling.

mcqs.q: Cooling a saturated solution lowers the solubility, so the solution becomes:
mcqs.why: Cooling lowers solubility; if the extra solute stays dissolved on slow, undisturbed cooling, the solution is supersaturated.

lessons.title: 6.3 Types of Solutions and Dilution of Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
Types of Solutions (by state of solute and solvent)

TypeExample
Solid in liquidSalt in water (salt solution)
Gas in gasAir (oxygen and other gases in nitrogen)
Solid in solidBrass (zinc in copper); alloys
Liquid in solidAmalgam (a metal in mercury)
Liquid in gasFog/mist (water droplets in air)
Liquid in liquidAlcohol in water (alcohol solution)
  • An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals — a solid-in-solid solution, e.g. brass: solute = zinc (smaller amount, 20%), solvent = copper (larger amount, 80%).
  • A heterogeneous mixture is one that is not uniform, e.g. water and sand, because sand does not dissolve in water.

Dilute and Concentrated Solutions

A dilute solution has little solute, whereas a concentrated solution has much solute. A concentrated solution can be made from a dilute solution by evaporating solvent or by adding more solute.

Dilution

Dilution means making a solution more dilute, i.e. adding solvent to it.

Formula: M1V1 = M2V2

Example: How much 4M stock solution is needed to make 200 ml of 0.5M solution?

M1V1 = M2V2 → 4 × V1 = 0.5 × 200 → V1 = 100 ÷ 4 = 25 ml

Example: Preparing 500 cm³ of 0.1M HNO3 from 10M HNO3:

10 × V1 = 0.1 × 500 → V1 = 5 cm³; take 5 cm³ of the 10M acid and dilute with water to 500 cm³.

mcqs.q: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of:
mcqs.why: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, i.e. a solid-in-solid solution, such as brass (zinc in copper).

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a heterogeneous mixture?
mcqs.why: Water and sand form a heterogeneous mixture because sand does not dissolve in water. Sugar, salt and alcohol dissolve to form homogeneous solutions.

mcqs.q: Which pair shows a solid dissolved in a liquid?
options: Solid-liquid, such as salt in water
mcqs.why: Salt in water is a solid-in-liquid solution: the solid salt is the solute and liquid water is the solvent.

mcqs.q: In which solution are both solute and solvent solids?
options: Solid in solid, such as an alloy
mcqs.why: In a solid-in-solid solution both components are solids, such as an alloy like brass (zinc in copper).

mcqs.q: Brass is a solid-in-solid solution. In brass (20% zinc, 80% copper):
options: Zinc is the solute and copper is the solvent
mcqs.why: In brass, zinc is the solute (smaller amount, 20%) and copper is the solvent (larger amount, 80%). It is a solid-in-solid solution (alloy).

mcqs.q: Fog or mist is an example of:
mcqs.why: Fog/mist consists of tiny water droplets in air, so it is a liquid-in-gas type of solution (a colloidal form of it).

mcqs.q: Alcohol in water is which type of solution?
mcqs.why: Alcohol in water is a liquid-in-liquid solution because both the solute (alcohol) and the solvent (water) are liquids.

mcqs.q: Air is which type of solution?
mcqs.why: Air is a gas-in-gas solution: oxygen and other gases are dissolved in nitrogen, which is present in the largest amount.

mcqs.q: A dilute solution differs from a concentrated solution because a dilute solution has:
mcqs.why: A dilute solution has little solute, whereas a concentrated solution has much solute in the same amount of solvent or solution.

mcqs.q: How can a concentrated solution be made from a dilute solution?
options: By evaporating solvent or adding more solute
mcqs.why: A concentrated solution can be made from a dilute solution by evaporating some solvent or by adding more solute. Adding solvent would dilute it further.

lessons.title: 6.4 Units of Concentration of Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
Concentration of a Solution

Concentration is the amount of solute in a given amount of solution or solvent. It can be expressed as percent or as molarity. A solution with lower molarity is more dilute: 2M is more dilute than 3M, and 0.25M has the least solute among 0.5M, 0.75M, 1.5M and 0.25M.

Percent Concentrations

  • (m/m)%: grams of solute in 100 g of solution. A 10% (m/m) sugar solution means 10 g sugar in 100 g solution, i.e. 10 g sugar + 90 g water.
  • (m/v)%: grams of solute in 100 cm³ of solution. Example: 5% (m/v) means 5 g solute in 100 cm³ of solution.
  • (v/v)%: volume of solute in 100 cm³ of solution, e.g. 20 cm³ alcohol + 80 cm³ water = 20% (v/v).

Molarity

Molarity is the number of moles of solute in 1 dm³ of solution. A molar solution is one in which 1 mole of solute is dissolved in 1 dm³ of solution, called 1M. Example: dissolving 40 g NaOH in 1 dm³ of solution makes a 1M NaOH solution.

Formulas: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in dm³; Mass = molarity × volume (dm³) × molar mass

Worked Examples

Example 1: Molarity of 40 g NaCl in 500 cm³ solution: moles = 40 ÷ 58.5 = 0.684; volume = 0.5 dm³; M = 0.684 ÷ 0.5 = 1.37M

Example 2: 1.25 g HCl made to 30 cm³: molar mass HCl = 36.5 g; moles = 1.25 ÷ 36.5 = 0.03425; volume = 0.030 dm³; molarity = 0.03425 ÷ 0.030 = 1.14M

Example 3: 2.5 g KCl in 100 cm³: molar mass KCl = 74.5 g; moles = 2.5 ÷ 74.5 = 0.03356; concentration = 0.03356 ÷ 0.1 = 0.34 mol/dm³

Example 4: NaOH in 1 dm³ of 0.5M solution: moles = 0.5 × 1 = 0.5; mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g

Example 5: NaOH needed for 400 cm³ of 0.3M: moles = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12; mass = 0.12 × 40 = 4.8 g

Example 6: 100 cm³ mineral water contains 28 g calcium: concentration = 28 ÷ 0.1 = 280 g/dm³

Example 7: % (m/m) of 10 g sugar in 140 g water: total = 150 g; % = 10 ÷ 150 × 100 = 6.67%

Example 8: A 1.2M NaOH solution: mass in 1 dm³ = 1.2 × 40 = 48 g/dm³; in 500 cm³ = 24 g

2 moles of NaCl = 2 × 58.5 = 117 g (molar mass of NaCl = 58.5 g).

mcqs.q: How many grams are 2 moles of NaCl (molar mass 58.5 g)?
mcqs.why: 1 mole of NaCl = 58.5 g, so 2 moles = 2 × 58.5 = 117 g.

mcqs.q: What is the molarity when 40 g NaCl is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution?
A 10% (m/m) sugar solution means 10 g sugar in how many grams of water?
mcqs.why: A 10% (m/m) solution has 10 g sugar in 100 g of solution, so the water is 100 − 10 = 90 g.

mcqs.q: Which solution has the least solute?
mcqs.why: 0.25M has the least solute because it is the lowest molarity — molarity shows the moles of solute per dm³ of solution.

mcqs.q: Mass/volume percent (m/v)% means:
options: Grams of solute in 100 cm³ of solution
Grams of solute in 100 g of solution
cm³ of solute in 100 cm³ solution
mcqs.why: (m/v)% means grams of solute in 100 cm³ of solution. Example: 5% (m/v) means 5 g solute in 100 cm³ of solution.

mcqs.q: A molar (1M) solution is one in which:
options: 1 mole of solute is dissolved in 1 dm³ of solution
mcqs.why: A molar solution has 1 mole of solute in 1 dm³ of solution, e.g. dissolving 40 g NaOH in 1 dm³ of solution makes 1M NaOH.

mcqs.q: The molarity of a solution made by dissolving 1.25 g HCl (molar mass 36.5 g) to 30 cm³ is:
How much NaOH is needed to prepare 400 cm³ of 0.3M solution (molar mass 40 g)?
20 cm³ alcohol is mixed with 80 cm³ water. The (v/v) concentration is:
Which solution is more dilute: 2M or 3M?
mcqs.why: The 2M solution is more dilute because its molarity (moles of solute per dm³) is lower than that of the 3M solution.

lessons.title: 6.5 Solubility
lessons.notes_html:
What is Solubility?

Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. When no more solute can dissolve in the solution, the solution is saturated and that is the limit of concentration.

Effect of Temperature on Solubility

The solubility of most solid solutes, such as salt, increases with temperature, because a hot solvent can dissolve more solute.

"Like Dissolves Like"

A solute dissolves because the solute-solvent attraction is stronger than the solute-solute and solvent-solvent forces. The general rule is "like dissolves like":

  • A polar solute dissolves in a polar solvent, and a non-polar solute dissolves in a non-polar solvent, because molecules with the same kind of intermolecular forces attract one another. Example: salt in water, grease in benzene.
  • Polar solutes dissolve only in polar solvents because the molecules of a polar solute attract the molecules of a polar solvent.
  • A polar solute cannot dissolve in a non-polar solvent, because the non-polar solvent cannot separate the strongly attracting polar solute particles.
  • Petrol is non-polar and water is polar, so petrol does not dissolve in water. Benzene is non-polar, so it also does not dissolve in water.
  • A non-polar solute does not dissolve in water because the polar water molecules attract one another strongly by hydrogen bonding, and a non-polar solute cannot break in between them.
  • If the solute-solvent attraction is stronger than the solute-solute attraction, a solution can form, because the solvent separates the solute particles and surrounds them.

mcqs.q: Solubility is shown as grams of solute per how many grams of solvent?
mcqs.why: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute (in grams) that dissolves in 100 grams of solvent at a given temperature.

mcqs.q: Solubility is defined as:
options: The maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature
mcqs.why: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature; beyond this the solution is saturated.

mcqs.q: How does the solubility of salt change with an increase in temperature?
options: It increases, because a hot solvent can dissolve more solute
mcqs.why: The solubility of most solid solutes such as salt increases with temperature, because a hot solvent can dissolve more solute.

mcqs.q: The rule "like dissolves like" means:
options: A polar solute dissolves in a polar solvent and a non-polar solute in a non-polar solvent
mcqs.why: Polar dissolves in polar and non-polar in non-polar, because molecules with the same kind of intermolecular forces attract one another; e.g. salt in water, grease in benzene.

mcqs.q: Why is petrol not soluble in water?
options: Petrol is non-polar and water is polar, so by "like dissolves like" it does not dissolve
mcqs.why: Petrol is non-polar and water is polar; substances of opposite polarity do not mix, so petrol does not dissolve in water.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene not dissolve in water?
options: Benzene is non-polar and water is polar
mcqs.why: Benzene is non-polar and water is polar, so benzene does not dissolve in water, following the rule "like dissolves like".

mcqs.q: Why do polar solutes dissolve only in polar solvents?
options: The molecules of a polar solute attract the molecules of a polar solvent
mcqs.why: By the rule "like dissolves like", the molecules of a polar solute attract the molecules of a polar solvent strongly, so they dissolve in it.

mcqs.q: A solute dissolves in a solvent when:
options: The solute-solvent attraction is stronger than the solute-solute and solvent-solvent forces
mcqs.why: A solute dissolves because the solute-solvent attraction is stronger than the solute-solute and solvent-solvent forces, so the solvent separates and surrounds the solute particles.

mcqs.q: Why does a non-polar solute not dissolve in water?
options: Polar water molecules attract one another strongly by hydrogen bonding, and a non-polar solute cannot break in between them
mcqs.why: The polar water molecules attract one another strongly by hydrogen bonding, and a non-polar solute cannot break in between them, so it does not dissolve.

mcqs.q: When a solution can dissolve no more solute at that temperature, it is:
options: Saturated, and that amount is the solubility limit
mcqs.why: When no more solute can dissolve, the solution is saturated and that maximum amount fixes the limit of concentration — the solubility.

lessons.title: 6.6 Comparison of Solution, Suspension and Colloids
lessons.notes_html:
Solution, Colloid and Suspension — Comparison

FeatureSolutionColloidSuspension
Particle sizeSmaller than 1 nm1 to 1000 nmLarger than 1000 nm
HomogeneityHomogeneousLess homogeneous; scatters lightHeterogeneous
SettlingParticles do not settleParticles do not settleParticles settle down
LightPasses throughScatters light (Tyndall effect)Scatters/blocks light

Colloids and the Tyndall Effect

  • The particles of a colloid scatter light, so the beam of light is visible in the colloid. This is called the Tyndall effect, like a car's light being visible in fog.
  • Colloid particles are very small and always in motion, so they do not settle at the bottom.
  • A colloidal solution is shaken well before use so that its particles spread evenly again.
  • Examples: milk (used as food), fog, starch solution. Glucose solution is a true solution, while starch solution is a colloidal solution.
  • A false (non-true) solution is one whose particles are larger than true-solution particles and which scatter light, such as a colloid or suspension.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a true solution (as given in the book)?
mcqs.why: According to the book, ink in water is the closest example of a true solution among the given options; starch and soap solutions are colloids and toothpaste is also not a true solution.

mcqs.q: What is the particle size in a true solution?
options: Less than 1 nm (the smallest, given as less than 10³ nm in the book's option)
mcqs.why: True-solution particles are smaller than 1 nm — the smallest of all mixtures — so a true solution is completely homogeneous and its particles never settle.

mcqs.q: The difference between a solution, a colloid and a suspension is mainly in:
options: Particle size: solution < 1 nm, colloid 1–1000 nm, suspension > 1000 nm
mcqs.why: Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm and never settle; colloid particles are 1 to 1000 nm, scatter light and do not settle; suspension particles are larger than 1000 nm and settle down.

mcqs.q: The Tyndall effect is:
options: Scattering of a beam of light by colloid particles, making the beam visible
mcqs.why: The particles of a colloid scatter light, so the path of a light beam becomes visible in the colloid — the Tyndall effect, like a car's light visible in fog.

mcqs.q: How is a colloid different from a solution?
options: Its particles are larger (1 to 1000 nm), it scatters light and looks less homogeneous
mcqs.why: Colloid particles are larger than solution particles (1 to 1000 nm), they scatter light (Tyndall effect) and look less homogeneous than a solution.

mcqs.q: Which is a colloidal solution: starch solution or glucose solution?
mcqs.why: Starch solution is a colloidal solution, whereas glucose solution is a true solution with particles smaller than 1 nm.

mcqs.q: Why do the particles of a colloid not settle?
options: They are very small and always in motion
mcqs.why: Colloid particles are very small and always in motion (Brownian motion), so they do not settle at the bottom, unlike suspension particles.

mcqs.q: Why is a colloidal solution shaken well before use?
options: To make it a true solution
To spread its particles evenly again
mcqs.why: Shaking spreads the colloid particles evenly through the whole solution again, so every part of it has the same composition.

mcqs.q: Milk and fog are examples of:
mcqs.why: Milk is a colloid used as food, and fog is also a colloid; both scatter light and their particles do not settle.

mcqs.q: A false (non-true) solution is one whose:
options: Particles are larger than true-solution particles and which scatters light, such as a colloid or suspension
Particles are invisible in every way
mcqs.why: A false solution has particles larger than true-solution particles and scatters light; colloids and suspensions are false solutions.

lessons.title: 7.1 Oxidation and Reduction
lessons.notes_html:
Oxidation and Reduction

  • Oxidation: losing electrons or gaining oxygen, e.g. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
  • Reduction: gaining electrons or losing oxygen, e.g. Cl2 + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Oxidation and reduction always happen together in a redox reaction.

Oxidising and Reducing Agents

  • Oxidising agent: the substance that takes electrons and oxidises another substance, e.g. Cl2, H2SO4, KMnO4.
  • Reducing agent: the substance that gives electrons and reduces another substance, e.g. Zn, Al, Na, H2S.
  • The oxidising agent itself is reduced, and the reducing agent itself is oxidised.

Identifying Agents in Equations

EquationOxidising agent (reduced)Reducing agent (oxidised)
Zn + Cl2 → ZnCl2Cl2Zn
Br2 + H2S → 2HBr + SBr2H2S
2Ca + O2 → 2CaOO2Ca
2Li + S → Li2SSLi
H2 + Cl2 → 2HClCl2H2

From the list Al, Na, H2S, H2SO4, KMnO4, Zn: oxidising agents are H2SO4 and KMnO4; reducing agents are Al, Na, H2S and Zn.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an oxidising agent?
mcqs.why: Cl2 is an oxidising agent because it takes electrons and oxidises another substance; in doing so, chlorine itself is reduced to Cl−.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reducing agent?
mcqs.why: Al (aluminium) is a reducing agent because it gives electrons and reduces another substance; aluminium itself is oxidised.

mcqs.q: Oxidation is:
mcqs.why: Oxidation is losing electrons or gaining oxygen, e.g. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Reduction is the opposite: gaining electrons or losing oxygen.

mcqs.q: Reduction is:
mcqs.why: Reduction is gaining electrons or losing oxygen, e.g. Cl2 + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻. The substance that gains electrons is reduced.

mcqs.q: An oxidising agent is a substance that:
options: Takes electrons and oxidises another substance
mcqs.why: An oxidising agent takes electrons and oxidises another substance, e.g. Cl2. The reducing agent gives electrons, e.g. Zn.

mcqs.q: In the equation Zn + Cl2 → ZnCl2, the reducing agent is:
mcqs.why: Zn is the reducing agent and the substance oxidised (it loses electrons). Cl2 is the oxidising agent and the substance reduced.

mcqs.q: In Br2 + H2S → 2HBr + S, the substance oxidised is:
mcqs.why: H2S is the reducing agent and the substance oxidised (it loses hydrogen/electrons). Br2 is the oxidising agent and is reduced to HBr.

mcqs.q: In 2Ca + O2 → 2CaO, oxygen is:
options: The oxidising agent and the substance reduced
mcqs.why: O2 is the oxidising agent and the substance reduced; Ca is the reducing agent and the substance oxidised, forming CaO.

mcqs.q: From Al, Na, H2S, H2SO4, KMnO4, Zn — the oxidising agents are:
mcqs.why: H2SO4 and KMnO4 are oxidising agents because they take electrons. Al, Na, H2S and Zn give electrons, so they are reducing agents.

mcqs.q: In H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, H2 is:
mcqs.why: H2 is the reducing agent and is oxidised; Cl2 is the oxidising agent and is reduced, forming 2HCl.

lessons.title: 7.2 Electrochemical Cells
lessons.notes_html:
Electrolytes

  • An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity in the molten or aqueous state through free ions.
  • A strong electrolyte dissociates fully into ions in water, e.g. HCl, NaOH, KCl.
  • A weak electrolyte ionises only slightly in water, e.g. CH3COOH (acetic acid), H2S, NH4OH.
  • A non-electrolyte does not produce ions and does not conduct electricity, e.g. glucose, urea, benzene. Urea is not an electrolyte.
  • Graphite is not an electrolyte because it conducts electricity through electrons, not ions.
  • Only ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten or aqueous state, because in these states their free ions can move and carry charge. In the solid state the ions are locked in place, so electricity cannot flow.

Electrochemical Cells

  • A voltaic (galvanic) cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy, such as the Daniel cell. An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a chemical reaction, such as the electrolysis of water.
  • Both have two electrodes (anode and cathode) and an electrolyte.
  • In a Daniel cell, zinc (Zn) is the anode and copper (Cu) is the cathode.
  • Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode. In an electrolytic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode (+) and reduction at the cathode (−); electrons flow from the anode to the cathode through the external circuit. K+ ions move to the cathode and Cl− ions to the anode in the electrolysis of KCl solution.

Dry Cell

In a dry cell, the zinc cover is the anode, the carbon rod in the middle is the cathode, and NH4Cl paste between them is the electrolyte. A chemical reaction produces electricity. It is used in torches, radios and toys.

Lead Storage Battery

A lead storage battery is a rechargeable battery with lead plates and sulphuric acid. On discharge, lead sulphate forms; on charging, lead and lead dioxide form again. It is used in vehicles.

Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis

  • First law: the mass of substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed.
  • Second law: when the same quantity of electricity is passed, the masses of different substances deposited are proportional to their equivalent weights.
  • One Faraday = 96500 coulombs of charge.
  • Equivalent weight = atomic mass ÷ valency. For aluminium: 27 ÷ 3 = 9 g.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not an electrolyte (it conducts through electrons, not ions)?
mcqs.why: Graphite is not an electrolyte because it conducts electricity through electrons, not ions. Electrolytes conduct through free ions in the molten or aqueous state.

mcqs.q: One Faraday equals how many coulombs?
mcqs.why: One Faraday equals 96500 coulombs — the charge on one mole of electrons, used in Faraday's laws of electrolysis.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not an electrolyte?
mcqs.why: Urea is not an electrolyte because it does not form ions in water. HCl, NaCl and KCl solutions conduct through free ions.

mcqs.q: Which forms a weak electrolyte with water?
mcqs.why: CH3COOH (acetic acid) is a weak electrolyte because it ionises only slightly in water. HCl, KOH and NaCl dissociate almost fully.

mcqs.q: In a Daniel cell, what is used as the cathode?
mcqs.why: In a Daniel cell, copper (Cu) is the cathode and zinc (Zn) is the anode. Reduction occurs at the cathode.

mcqs.q: What is the equivalent weight of aluminium (atomic mass 27, valency 3)?
mcqs.why: Equivalent weight = atomic mass ÷ valency = 27 ÷ 3 = 9 g. This is used in Faraday's second law of electrolysis.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Reduction and oxidation both occur at the anode
Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode
mcqs.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode in electrochemical cells. This rule applies to both voltaic and electrolytic cells.

mcqs.q: An electrolyte is a substance that:
options: Conducts electricity in the molten or aqueous state through free ions
mcqs.why: An electrolyte conducts electricity in the molten or aqueous state through free ions, e.g. NaCl solution. In the solid state its ions are locked in place.

mcqs.q: A strong electrolyte is one that:
options: Dissociates fully into ions in water, e.g. HCl, NaOH, KCl
mcqs.why: A strong electrolyte dissociates fully into ions in water, e.g. HCl, KCl, NaOH. Weak electrolytes like CH3COOH and NH4OH ionise only slightly.

mcqs.q: In a dry cell, the anode and cathode are:
mcqs.why: In a dry cell the zinc cover is the anode and the carbon rod in the middle is the cathode, with NH4Cl paste as the electrolyte. Dry cells are used in torches, radios and toys.

lessons.title: 7.3 Corrosion and its Prevention
lessons.notes_html:
Rusting (Corrosion)

Rusting is iron reacting with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust). Machines and iron objects are damaged by rust.

Protection from Rusting

  • Painting the surface.
  • Greasing or oiling.
  • Galvanising — coating iron with zinc.
  • Electroplating with another metal.

Electroplating

Electroplating deposits a thin layer of one metal on another object using electricity. The steps are:

  • Step 1: The object to be plated is cleaned.
  • Step 2: It is made the cathode.
  • Step 3: The plating metal is made the anode.
  • Step 4: Both are dipped in an electrolyte (a solution of the plating metal's salt) and current is passed, so the metal deposits on the cathode (the object).

Examples

  • Tin or zinc on iron: the iron object is made the cathode and tin or zinc the anode; both are dipped in a solution of that metal's salt and current is passed, so tin or zinc deposits on the iron.
  • Silver plating: the object is made the cathode and silver the anode; both are dipped in a solution of a silver salt (such as silver nitrate) and current is passed, so silver deposits on the object.

mcqs.q: Rusting is:
options: Iron reacting with oxygen and water to form iron oxide
mcqs.why: Rusting is the corrosion of iron: iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust), which damages machines and objects.

mcqs.q: Which is a method to protect iron from rusting?
mcqs.why: Iron is protected from rusting by painting, greasing, galvanising (zinc coating) and electroplating, which keep air and water away from its surface.

mcqs.q: Galvanising means coating iron with:
mcqs.why: Galvanising is coating iron with zinc, which protects the iron from rusting even if the coating is scratched.

mcqs.q: In electroplating, the object to be plated is made the:
mcqs.why: The object to be plated is made the cathode; the plating metal is the anode, and metal ions deposit on the cathode when current passes.

mcqs.q: The first step of electroplating is:
options: Cleaning the object to be plated
mcqs.why: First the object to be plated is cleaned. Then it is made the cathode, the plating metal the anode, and both are dipped in the electrolyte.

mcqs.q: To electroplate silver on an object, the anode is made of:
mcqs.why: For silver plating, the object is the cathode and silver is the anode; both are dipped in a solution of a silver salt such as silver nitrate, and silver deposits on the object.

mcqs.q: Tin and zinc can be electroplated on an iron surface by making the iron object the:
options: Cathode, with tin or zinc as the anode in its salt solution
mcqs.why: The iron object is made the cathode and tin or zinc the anode; in a solution of that metal's salt, current deposits tin or zinc on the iron.

mcqs.q: During electroplating, the metal deposits on the:
mcqs.why: Positively charged metal ions move to the cathode and deposit there as metal, so the coating forms on the object connected as cathode.

mcqs.q: Electroplating protects iron objects because the coating:
options: Covers the surface and keeps air and water away, preventing rust
mcqs.why: A plated metal layer covers the iron surface, keeping oxygen and water away; zinc and tin coatings are used to protect iron from rusting.

mcqs.q: Rust is chemically:
options: Iron oxide formed by iron with oxygen and water
mcqs.why: Rust is iron oxide, formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water. It is prevented by painting, greasing, galvanising and plating.

lessons.title: 7.4 Alloy Formation
lessons.notes_html:
What is an Alloy?

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals (a solid-in-solid solution). Alloys are made to improve the properties of metals, such as strength and resistance to rusting.

Common Alloys

AlloyComposition
BrassCu–Zn (copper + zinc)
BronzeCu–Sn (copper + tin)
SteelFe–C (iron + carbon)
DuraluminNi–Mg–Al–Cu
Bell metalA copper–tin alloy

mcqs.q: What is the Cu–Sn alloy called?
mcqs.why: The Cu–Sn alloy (copper + tin) is called bronze. Brass is the Cu–Zn alloy.

mcqs.q: Brass is an alloy of:
mcqs.why: Brass is the alloy of copper and zinc (Cu–Zn). Bronze is copper and tin, and steel is iron and carbon.

mcqs.q: An alloy is:
options: A compound of metal and acid
A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals
A mixture of metal and water
mcqs.why: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals — a solid-in-solid solution — such as brass, bronze and steel.

mcqs.q: Duralumin contains:
mcqs.why: Duralumin is the alloy with composition Ni–Mg–Al–Cu. It is light and strong, like other useful alloys.

mcqs.q: Steel is an alloy of:
mcqs.why: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon (Fe–C). Adding carbon makes iron harder and stronger.

mcqs.q: Bronze contains the metals:
mcqs.why: Bronze is Cu–Sn: copper and tin. The alloy Sn–Zn–Cu given in the book is also classed with bronze-type alloys.

mcqs.q: Alloys are prepared to:
options: Improve the properties of metals, such as strength and rust resistance
mcqs.why: Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of metals made to improve properties such as strength, hardness and resistance to corrosion.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an alloy?
mcqs.why: Brass (Cu–Zn) is an alloy — a homogeneous mixture of two metals. Pure copper is a single metal, not an alloy.

mcqs.q: An alloy is an example of which type of solution?
mcqs.why: An alloy is a solid-in-solid solution because both the solute and solvent are solids mixed uniformly, e.g. zinc in copper (brass).

mcqs.q: The alloy of copper and zinc used for utensils and fittings is:
mcqs.why: Brass is the Cu–Zn alloy. Bronze is Cu–Sn and duralumin contains Ni–Mg–Al–Cu.

lessons.title: 8.1 Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Metals

  • Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable and ductile.
  • They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
  • They are sonorous and have high melting points.
  • Metals give electrons to form positive ions (cations), e.g. Na → Na+ + e−. That is why metals conduct electricity and form ionic compounds.
  • Most metals are solids, but mercury (Hg) and gallium (Ga) are found in the liquid state.

Alkali Metals (Group IA)

Alkali metals are the very reactive metals of Group IA: lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), francium (Fr). They are not found free in nature because they are very reactive and react quickly with air and water, so they cannot stay in the free state and occur only in compounds.

Alkaline-Earth Metals (Group IIA)

Alkaline-earth metals are the metals of Group IIA: beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg), calcium (Ca), strontium (Sr), barium (Ba), radium (Ra). From the list Sr, Sb, Si, Se, B, Ba, Br, Bi — Ba and Sr are the alkaline-earth metals.

Soft Metals and Hard Metals

PropertySodium (soft metal)Iron (hard metal)
Mohs hardness0.54.5
Melting point98°C1535°C
Boiling point890°C2450°C
Density0.971 g/cm³7.87 g/cm³

Soft metals can be cut with a knife and have low hardness and melting points, such as Na, K, Rb, Cs. Hard metals have high hardness and melting points and strong metallic bonding, such as Ni, Fe, W.

Cations and Anions

  • Cation: a positive ion, e.g. Na+ and Ca²⁺.
  • Anion: a negative ion, e.g. Cl− and O²⁻.

Noble Metals

Noble metals such as gold, silver and platinum do not react easily with other substances, because they are chemically stable and are not affected by air, water and acids. Noble metals: gold (Au), silver (Ag), platinum (Pt), iridium (Ir), osmium (Os), ruthenium (Ru), rhodium (Rh), palladium (Pd).

Importance of Silver and Gold

  • Silver: a very good conductor of heat and electricity; used in jewellery, coins, utensils, photography, electronics and medicines. It is a noble metal and does not rust easily. Silver nitrate (AgNO3) is called lunar caustic.
  • Gold: a shiny, soft, malleable and rust-free metal; used in jewellery, coins, dentistry, electronics and space technology. An astronaut's helmet visor is coated with gold because gold reflects infrared/solar radiation and protects from heat. Gold is used in mirror glass because it is highly reflective and does not tarnish. In dentistry, gold is used in fillings and crowns because it is inert, non-corrosive and biocompatible.
  • Platinum is used as a catalyst: it speeds up reactions without being consumed, e.g. in catalytic converters and the Ostwald process.

Importance of Sodium and Magnesium

  • Sodium (Group IA alkali metal): used in salt, soda, soap, glass and chemical industries; it also plays an important role in the body.
  • Magnesium (Group IIA alkaline-earth metal): important in light strong alloys, fireworks, medicines and as part of chlorophyll in plants. Its uses include alloys, fireworks/flares, medicine (antacid), chlorophyll and sacrificial protection.

Uses of Some Compounds

  • Washing soda (Na2CO3): cleaning, water softening, making glass and soap.
  • Bleach (Ca(OCl)2): disinfectant and whitening.
  • Sodium nitrate (NaNO3): fertiliser, food preservation, glass.
  • Lime: cement, mortar, whitewash, steel. Gypsum/plaster: plaster of Paris, wallboard, cement. Calcium tungstate: fluorescent lamps, X-ray screens.

Classification Practice

From Ge, Ba, P, K, Si, Sr, S, Sb, Ca, C — metalloids: Ge, Si, Sb; metals: Ba, K, Sr, Ca; non-metals: P, S, C.

mcqs.q: Which metal belongs with the alkaline-earth metals?
mcqs.why: Ba (barium) is a Group IIA alkaline-earth metal. B is a metalloid, Bi a metal of another group, and Br a non-metal.

mcqs.q: Silver nitrate, called Lunar Caustic, has the formula:
mcqs.why: Silver nitrate is AgNO3, the compound called lunar caustic. Silver is a noble metal and a very good conductor of electricity.

mcqs.q: Which metals are found in the liquid state?
mcqs.why: Mercury (Hg) and gallium (Ga) are the metals found in the liquid state; almost all other metals are solids.

mcqs.q: Alkali metals are not found free in nature because:
options: They are very reactive and react quickly with air and water
mcqs.why: Alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) are very reactive; they react quickly with air and water, so they occur only in compounds, never free.

mcqs.q: Noble metals such as gold and platinum are inert because:
options: They are chemically stable and not affected by air, water and acids
mcqs.why: Noble metals do not react easily with other substances because they are chemically stable and unaffected by air, water and acids.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a noble metal?
mcqs.why: Gold (Au) is a noble metal, along with silver (Ag), platinum (Pt), iridium (Ir), osmium (Os), ruthenium (Ru), rhodium (Rh) and palladium (Pd).

mcqs.q: Metals form cations because they:
options: Give electrons to form positive ions, e.g. Na → Na+ + e−
mcqs.why: Metals give electrons to form positive ions (cations). That is why metals conduct electricity and form ionic compounds.

mcqs.q: A cation is:
options: A positive ion, e.g. Na+ and Ca²⁺
mcqs.why: A cation is a positive ion, e.g. Na+ and Ca²⁺. An anion is a negative ion, e.g. Cl− and O²⁻.

mcqs.q: Sodium is a soft metal that can be cut with a knife. Its melting point and density are:
mcqs.why: Sodium: melting point 98°C, boiling point 890°C, density 0.971 g/cm³, Mohs hardness 0.5. Iron is a hard metal: melting point 1535°C, density 7.87 g/cm³, hardness 4.5.

mcqs.q: Hard metals such as Ni, Fe and W have:
options: High hardness and melting points with strong metallic bonding
mcqs.why: Hard metals have high hardness and melting points and strong metallic bonding, unlike soft metals such as Na, K, Rb, Cs which can be cut with a knife.

mcqs.q: Gold is used in dentistry for fillings and crowns because it is:
mcqs.why: Gold is inert, non-corrosive and biocompatible (not harmful to the body), so it is used in dental fillings and crowns.

mcqs.q: An astronaut's helmet visor is coated with gold because gold:
options: Reflects infrared/solar radiation and protects from heat
mcqs.why: Gold reflects infrared and solar radiation and protects the astronaut from heat; gold is also highly reflective and does not tarnish, so it is used on mirror glass.

mcqs.q: Platinum is used as a catalyst because it:
options: Speeds up reactions without being consumed, e.g. in catalytic converters and the Ostwald process
mcqs.why: Platinum speeds up reactions without being consumed itself, so it is used as a catalyst in catalytic converters and the Ostwald process.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is important because it is used in:
options: Light strong alloys, fireworks, medicines and chlorophyll in plants
mcqs.why: Magnesium is a Group IIA alkaline-earth metal used in light strong alloys, fireworks, medicines (antacid), sacrificial protection, and it is part of chlorophyll in plants.

mcqs.q: Washing soda (Na2CO3) is used for:
options: Cleaning, water softening, making glass and soap
mcqs.why: Washing soda is used in cleaning, water softening and making glass and soap. Bleach is a disinfectant and sodium nitrate is a fertiliser.

lessons.title: 8.2 Non-Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Non-Metals

  • Non-metals are dull (not shiny) and brittle.
  • They are poor conductors of electricity.
  • They have low melting and boiling points.
  • They gain electrons to form anions, and form acidic oxides.
  • Non-metals attract electrons strongly, so their electronegativity is high. Fluorine is the most electronegative element. They lack metallic properties: not shiny, not conductors, brittle.
  • Chlorine (Cl) acts as an oxidising agent in a chemical reaction because it takes electrons and oxidises another substance.

Halogens (Group VIIA)

Halogens are the reactive non-metals of Group VIIA: fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I), astatine (At). They are very reactive because their outer shell has 7 electrons and taking one electron completes the octet. Reactivity decreases from top to bottom: F > Cl > Br > I.

  • Only fluorine, being above chlorine and more reactive, can displace chlorine.
  • Iodine (I2) is the halogen found in the solid state; bromine (Br2) is a liquid; F2 and Cl2 are gases.
  • Acidity of halogen acids increases in the order: HF < HCl < HBr < HI, i.e. HF is the weakest and HI is the strongest acid.

Noble Gases (Group VIIIA)

The non-metals of Group VIIIA are found in the gaseous state — the noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). From N, Na, Ni, Ne, Ar, At, He — the Group VIIIA elements are Ne, Ar and He. Group VIIIA is the group that has only non-metals in the gaseous state.

Metalloids

Metalloids show properties between metals and non-metals. The book's metalloid list is: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po, At. (Note: in the book's question, Se is the closest choice classed as a metalloid in some references.) Any three: boron (B), silicon (Si), germanium (Ge).

Group VA Non-Metals

Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), arsenic (As), antimony (Sb), bismuth (Bi).

Tests and Special Facts

  • CO2 test: carbon dioxide turns limewater milky because it combines with limewater to form calcium carbonate.
  • Chloride test (Cl−): adding silver nitrate to the solution gives a white precipitate.
  • Iodide test (I−): adding silver nitrate gives a yellow precipitate.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-metal?
mcqs.why: Br (bromine) is a halogen non-metal. Be and Ba are metals and B is a metalloid.

mcqs.q: Chlorine can be displaced by which halogen?
mcqs.why: Chlorine can be displaced only by fluorine (F), because fluorine is above chlorine in the group and is more reactive: F > Cl > Br > I.

mcqs.q: Which is the strongest acid among the halogen acids?
mcqs.why: HI is the strongest acid because the acidity of halogen acids increases in the order HF < HCl < HBr < HI; HF is the weakest.

mcqs.q: Which halogen is found in the solid state?
mcqs.why: I2 (iodine) is a solid halogen. Chlorine is a gas and bromine (Br2) is a liquid.

mcqs.q: The non-metals of which group are found in the gaseous state?
mcqs.why: Group VIIIA non-metals — the noble gases He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn — are found in the gaseous state.

mcqs.q: Which acts as an oxidising agent in a chemical reaction?
mcqs.why: Cl (chlorine) acts as an oxidising agent because it takes electrons and oxidises another substance. Be, Mg and Na are metals that give electrons.

mcqs.q: Which gas turns limewater milky?
mcqs.why: CO2 turns limewater milky because it combines with limewater to form calcium carbonate. This is the test for carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Halogens are very reactive because:
options: Their outer shell has 7 electrons, and taking one electron completes the octet
mcqs.why: Halogens have 7 electrons in the outer shell; by taking one electron they complete the octet, so they are very reactive. Reactivity decreases down the group: F > Cl > Br > I.

mcqs.q: The order of reactivity of halogens is:
mcqs.why: Halogen reactivity decreases from top to bottom of Group VIIA: F > Cl > Br > I. That is why only fluorine can displace chlorine.

mcqs.q: The halogens are the elements of group:
options: VIIA — F, Cl, Br, I, At
mcqs.why: Halogens are the reactive non-metals of Group VIIA: fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I) and astatine (At).

mcqs.q: Non-metals have high electronegativity, and the most electronegative element is:
mcqs.why: Non-metals attract electrons strongly, so their electronegativity is high. Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all.

mcqs.q: The test for chloride ions (Cl−) with silver nitrate gives:
mcqs.why: Adding silver nitrate to a chloride solution gives a white precipitate. For iodide ions (I−) the precipitate is yellow.

mcqs.q: The test for iodide ions (I−) with silver nitrate gives:
mcqs.why: Adding silver nitrate to an iodide solution gives a yellow precipitate (silver iodide). Chloride gives a white precipitate instead.

mcqs.q: From N, Na, Ni, Ne, Ar, At, He — the Group VIIIA elements are:
mcqs.why: Ne, Ar and He are the Group VIIIA (noble gas) elements. Na and Ni are metals, and At is a halogen/metalloid.
